misconceptions.actually: The digits are constrained by place value and carrying — usually only one assignment is consistent, found by elimination.

realWorldExamples.title: Splitting an odd bill in two
realWorldExamples.body: Three friends each chip in an odd number of rupees and wonder if the total can split evenly between two people. Parity answers instantly: three odds sum to an odd total, and an odd number of rupees can't divide into two equal whole-rupee shares. No arithmetic needed — just parity.

realWorldExamples.title: Fibonacci in a sunflower
realWorldExamples.body: Count the spirals on a sunflower head and you'll almost always get Virahāṅka–Fibonacci numbers — 34 one way, 55 the other. The same sequence Indian poets found counting syllable rhythms governs how a plant packs seeds most efficiently. Mathematics, poetry and biology meeting in one flower.

realWorldExamples.title: Codebreaking by elimination
realWorldExamples.body: Cracking a cryptarithm like SEND + MORE = MONEY uses the same constrain-and-eliminate logic that codebreakers and puzzle apps rely on: each column gives a clue, carries link the columns, and impossible digits get ruled out until one solution remains.

ncertQA.question: In the 'taller children in front' game, is the statement 'If a person says 0, then they are the tallest in the group' always, sometimes, or never true?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Sometimes true. Saying 0 only means no TALLER child stands IN FRONT; a taller child could stand behind them. So they may or may not be the tallest.

ncertQA.question: Can five number-cards, each odd, sum to 30? Why or why not?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: No. The sum of five odd numbers is odd (an odd count of odds gives an odd total), but 30 is even. So it is impossible.

ncertQA.question: What kind of number do you get when you add several even numbers? Several odd numbers?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Adding even numbers always gives an even number. Adding odd numbers gives an even number if there is an even count of them, and an odd number if there is an odd count.

ncertQA.question: Show that the sum of two odd numbers is always even.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Write the odds as 2m+1 and 2n+1. Their sum is 2m+2n+2 = 2(m+n+1), a multiple of 2, hence even. This holds for all m, n, so it is a proof.

ncertQA.question: Write the next three terms of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Each term is the sum of the previous two: 13+21=34, 21+34=55, 34+55=89. So the next three terms are 34, 55, 89.

ncertQA.question: In how many ways can 4 beats be filled with short (1-beat) and long (2-beat) syllables?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: 5 ways. The count satisfies F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2): F(3)=3, F(2)=2, so F(4)=3+2=5. (The rhythms are SSSS, SSL, SLS, LSS, LL.)

ncertQA.question: Solve T + T + T = UT, where the answer's units digit equals T.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: 3T must end in T, so 2T is a multiple of 10, giving T = 0 or 5. T = 0 gives a one-digit sum, so T = 5: 5+5+5 = 15, with U = 1.

ncertQA.question: Who first discovered the sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … and in what context?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Indian scholars such as Pingala and later Virahāṅka described it centuries before Fibonacci, while studying the rhythms of poetry — counting how many arrangements of short and long syllables fill a given number of beats. Hence it is called the Virahāṅka–Fibonacci sequence.

miniProjects.title: Parity Detective
needs: A handful of coins or counters
steps: Grab any handful of coins and split them into pairs. If none are left over, the count is even; if one is left over, it's odd.
Take two odd handfuls, combine them, and pair again — record whether the total is even or odd.
Repeat with three odd handfuls, then four. Note the pattern.
Now predict, WITHOUT counting, the parity of a sum of seven odd handfuls. Then check.
Try to write the reason as a sentence: 'An odd number of odd groups gives a ___ total because ___.'
miniProjects.expectedObservation: You'll find an even count of odd handfuls always pairs up perfectly (even total), while an odd count always leaves one stranded (odd total) — and you can predict it before counting.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Each odd group is 'pairs plus one leftover'. When you combine groups, the leftovers try to pair with each other; an even number of leftovers pairs perfectly, an odd number strands one. So the parity of the total depends only on how many odd groups there are — a parity argument, made with coins.

chapters.title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
chapters.summary: A triangle is the simplest closed shape — three corners (vertices), three sides, three angles. This chapter explores what side lengths can actually form a triangle (the triangle inequality: any two sides must together exceed the third), how to construct triangles with a compass and ruler, what an altitude is, and how triangles are classified — by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse).

topics.title: Triangle Basics
topics.summary: A triangle ∆ABC has three vertices (A, B, C), three sides joining them, and three angles (∠A, ∠B, ∠C). Vertices can be named in any order. If the three points lie on a straight line, no triangle forms.

concepts.title: Vertices, sides and angles of a triangle

explanations.oneLine: A triangle is a closed shape with three vertices (corner points), three sides (segments joining them), and three angles.
explanations.kidFriendly: A triangle is the most basic closed shape. It has three corner points called vertices (like A, B, C), three sides — line segments joining the pairs of vertices (AB, BC, CA), and three angles where the sides meet (∠A, ∠B, ∠C). We write it with a small triangle symbol: ∆ABC. You can name the vertices in any order — ∆ABC, ∆BCA, ∆CAB all mean the same triangle. One catch: if the three points happen to lie on a single straight line, the 'sides' flatten out and you get no triangle at all — you need three points NOT in a line.
explanations.textbook: A triangle consists of three non-collinear vertices, three sides (the segments joining each pair of vertices), and three interior angles formed where pairs of sides meet at the vertices. It is denoted ∆ABC, with the vertices nameable in any order. The angles ∠CAB, ∠ABC, ∠BCA are abbreviated ∠A, ∠B, ∠C. Three collinear points do not form a triangle (degenerate case).
explanations.expert: A triangle is the 2-simplex: the convex hull of three affinely independent (non-collinear) points in the plane. Affine independence is exactly the non-collinearity condition; collinear points give a degenerate simplex of lower dimension. The triangle is the foundational polygon — every polygon triangulates into triangles, making the triangle the basic unit of planar geometry and computer graphics meshes.

concepts.reasoning: Three points, if not in a straight line, are joined by three segments enclosing a region — that's a triangle. The corners are vertices, the segments are sides, and the openings between sides at each corner are the angles. Collinear points can't enclose anything, so they make no triangle.

useCases.title: Roof truss
useCases.description: A triangular truss has three vertices and three rigid sides — strong and stable.

useCases.title: Traffic 'yield' sign
useCases.description: A triangle with three vertices and three sides — the basic warning shape.

useCases.title: Samosa
useCases.description: A samosa's outline is roughly a triangle: three corners, three edges.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The triangle is special because it's RIGID — fix the three side lengths and the shape can't flex, unlike a four-sided frame which can collapse into a parallelogram. That's why bridges, cranes, and roof trusses are built from triangles: three sides lock the shape. This rigidity is also why triangles are the building block of all computer-graphics 3D models.
concepts.mnemonic: Three non-line points → three sides → a triangle ∆ABC with three angles.
concepts.predictQuestion: What three things make up a triangle, and what happens if the three corner points lie on one straight line?
whyChain: A triangle is built from three points that are NOT in a straight line. Join each pair of points with a segment and you get three sides; the corners where they meet are the three vertices; the openings at each corner are the three angles. Written ∆ABC.

The non-collinear condition is essential. If the three points DO lie on a single straight line, the would-be sides collapse onto that line and enclose no region — there's no triangle, just a flat segment. You need the three points spread out, not in a row.

This humble shape is the foundation of geometry. The triangle is RIGID — its three fixed sides lock the shape so it can't flex, which is why trusses, bridges and cranes are full of triangles. And because every polygon can be cut into triangles, the triangle is the basic unit from which all planar shapes — and all 3D computer-graphics models — are built.

questions.prompt: Name the three vertices, three sides and three angles of triangle ∆ABC. Can the three vertices lie on a straight line?
questions.answer: Vertices: A, B, C. Sides: AB, BC, CA. Angles: ∠A, ∠B, ∠C. No — three collinear points cannot form a triangle.
solutionSteps: Vertices are the three corner points: A, B, C.
Sides are the segments joining pairs: AB, BC, CA.
If A, B, C lie on one line, the sides flatten and enclose no area — no triangle.
commonMistakes: Listing only two sides or angles.
Thinking any three points form a triangle (collinear ones don't).

variations.prompt: How many sides and angles does any triangle have?
solutionSteps: By definition a triangle has 3 sides and 3 angles.

variations.answer: Yes — vertices can be named in any order.
solutionSteps: Order of naming doesn't change the triangle.

topics.title: The Triangle Inequality
topics.summary: Not every set of three lengths can form a triangle. The triangle inequality says: the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third. So 3, 4, 5 works, but 10, 15, 30 does not — because 10 + 15 = 25 is less than 30, and the two short sides can't reach across.

concepts.title: The triangle inequality

explanations.oneLine: Three lengths form a triangle only if the sum of every two of them is greater than the third — the triangle inequality.
explanations.kidFriendly: Can any three lengths make a triangle? No! Try 10, 15, 30. The two shorter sides (10 and 15) add to 25 — but the third side is 30. The short sides aren't long enough to reach across and meet; they fall short by 5. The rule, called the triangle inequality, says: for a triangle to exist, the sum of any two sides must be GREATER than the third side. 3, 4, 5 works (3+4 = 7 > 5, and the others too). 10, 15, 30 fails (10+15 = 25 < 30). It's enough to check that the two SHORTEST sides together beat the longest one.
explanations.textbook: The triangle inequality states that three positive lengths a, b, c can be the sides of a triangle if and only if the sum of every pair exceeds the third: a+b>c, b+c>a, and c+a>b. Equivalently, it suffices that the sum of the two smallest exceeds the largest. Lengths failing this (e.g., 10, 15, 30 since 10+15<30) cannot form a triangle; the two shorter sides cannot meet.
explanations.expert: The triangle inequality |a−b| < c < a+b is the metric-space axiom d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y)+d(y,z) realised geometrically: the straight path (one side) is never longer than a detour through a third vertex (the other two sides). It characterises realisable Euclidean triangles and underlies the definition of any metric/norm; equality a+b=c corresponds to the degenerate collinear case.

concepts.reasoning: To close up into a triangle, the two shorter sides, swung down from the ends of the longest side, must actually reach each other and overlap. If together they're shorter than the longest side, they can't span the gap, so no triangle closes.

useCases.title: Choosing sticks for a frame
useCases.description: Sticks 10, 15, 30 cm won't form a triangular frame — the short two can't span the long one.

useCases.title: GPS shortest path
useCases.description: Going direct (one side) is always shorter than detouring via a third point (two sides).

useCases.title: Compass construction
useCases.description: Two arcs from the ends of the base only intersect when the inequality holds.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The triangle inequality is one of the most important facts in all of mathematics — it defines what 'distance' means in every space, from flat geometry to the abstract spaces used in machine learning. 'The shortest distance between two points is a straight line' is just the triangle inequality in disguise.
concepts.mnemonic: Sum of any two sides > the third. Check: do the two shortest beat the longest?
concepts.predictQuestion: Can the lengths 10, 15 and 30 form a triangle?
whyChain: For three lengths to close into a triangle, the two shorter sides — swung down from the ends of the longest side — must actually reach across and meet. If they're too short combined, they never touch and no triangle forms.

That's the triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides must exceed the third. The decisive check is the two SHORTEST against the longest. For 10, 15, 30: the short sides sum to 10 + 15 = 25, which is LESS than 30. They fall 5 short of spanning the long side, so they can never meet — no triangle. (Compare 3, 4, 5: 3+4 = 7 > 5, so it works.)

This rule is far bigger than triangles. It's the formal definition of 'distance' in every mathematical space: a direct path between two points is never longer than a detour through a third. 'The shortest distance between two points is a straight line' is exactly the triangle inequality — making this one of the most fundamental facts in all of mathematics.

questions.prompt: Do the lengths 10, 15, 30 satisfy the triangle inequality? Can they form a triangle?
questions.answer: No. 10 + 15 = 25, which is less than 30, so the inequality fails and no triangle can be formed.
solutionSteps: Check the two shortest against the longest: 10 + 15 = 25.
Since the sum of the two shorter sides is NOT greater than the third, the inequality fails.
commonMistakes: Only checking one pair that happens to work (e.g. 15+30 > 10) and ignoring the failing pair.
Allowing equality (sum = third) as a triangle — it gives a flat, degenerate line.

solutionSteps: Two shorter sides sum to 14, less than 15.

questions.prompt: A triangle has two sides of length 8 cm and 5 cm. Between what values must the third side lie?
questions.answer: Greater than 3 cm and less than 13 cm (i.e. 3 < third side < 13).
solutionSteps: Difference condition: third side > 8 − 5 = 3 (so the other pairs' inequalities hold).
So the third side must satisfy 3 cm < side < 13 cm.
commonMistakes: Only applying the sum rule and forgetting the lower bound from the difference.
Including the endpoints 3 and 13 (those give degenerate flat triangles).

variations.prompt: Two sides are 6 and 6. Range for the third?
Two sides are 10 and 4. Range for the third?

topics.title: Constructing Triangles & Altitudes
topics.summary: Given three valid side lengths, you can construct the triangle with a compass: draw the base, then swing an arc of each remaining side-length from each base endpoint — where the arcs cross is the third vertex. An altitude is the perpendicular dropped from a vertex to the opposite side.

concepts.title: Constructing a triangle from its sides

explanations.oneLine: To construct a triangle from three side lengths, draw one side as a base, then swing an arc of each other length from each end; the arcs cross at the third vertex.
explanations.kidFriendly: Say you want ∆ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm. Step 1: draw the base AB = 4 cm. Step 2: from A, open the compass to 5 cm and draw an arc. Step 3: from B, open to 6 cm and draw an arc crossing the first. Step 4: where the arcs meet is C — join AC and BC. Why does the crossing point work? Any point on the arc from A is exactly 5 cm from A; any point on the arc from B is exactly 6 cm from B. The crossing point is BOTH — so it's exactly the right distances from A and B. This only works if the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality (otherwise the arcs never meet).
explanations.textbook: Triangle construction from three sides (SSS) uses compass arcs: draw the base of one given length, then from each endpoint draw an arc of radius equal to one of the remaining sides; their intersection is the third vertex. A point on an arc centred at A with radius r is exactly distance r from A, so the intersection simultaneously satisfies both distance requirements. The construction succeeds iff the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality (arcs intersect).
explanations.expert: The SSS construction realises the fact that three side lengths satisfying the triangle inequality determine a triangle uniquely up to congruence (the SSS congruence criterion). Each arc is a circle (locus of points at fixed distance from a centre); two circles intersect in 0, 1, or 2 points, and intersection in 2 points (reflections across the base) occurs precisely when |r₁−r₂| < AB < r₁+r₂ — the triangle inequality again.

concepts.reasoning: An arc drawn from a point with the compass marks every spot at exactly that distance from the point. Drawing two such arcs — one for each remaining side — finds the spot that is simultaneously the right distance from both base ends. That spot must be the third vertex.

useCases.title: Carpentry layout
useCases.description: A carpenter marks a triangular brace by swinging two tape-measure arcs to fix the apex.

useCases.title: Garden design
useCases.description: Laying out a triangular flowerbed with string arcs from two pegs finds the third corner.

useCases.title: Compass geometry
useCases.description: Classic ruler-and-compass construction of any triangle from three sides.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Ruler-and-compass construction is an ancient Greek art with deep limits — some constructions (like trisecting an arbitrary angle, or 'squaring the circle') were proven IMPOSSIBLE with only these tools, two thousand years after the questions were first asked. The humble compass arc you use here connects to some of the deepest results in mathematics.
concepts.mnemonic: Two arcs, one per remaining side, swung from the base ends. Where they cross = third vertex.
concepts.predictQuestion: To construct ∆ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm, where does the third vertex C come from?
whyChain: Start by drawing the base, AB = 4 cm. Now you need point C, which must be exactly 5 cm from A and exactly 6 cm from B at the same time. How do you find a point meeting both conditions?

Use arcs. Every point on an arc drawn from A with radius 5 cm is exactly 5 cm from A; every point on an arc from B with radius 6 cm is exactly 6 cm from B. The point where the two arcs CROSS satisfies both distances simultaneously — so it must be vertex C. Join AC and BC and the triangle is done.

This only works when the side lengths obey the triangle inequality — otherwise the two arcs are too far apart to ever meet, and (just as the inequality predicts) no triangle exists. The construction also shows that three side lengths fix a triangle's shape completely, which is the SSS congruence idea: same three sides, same triangle.

concepts.title: Altitudes of a triangle

explanations.oneLine: An altitude is the perpendicular segment from a vertex straight down to the opposite side (or its extension).
explanations.kidFriendly: An altitude of a triangle is the straight, perpendicular drop from a vertex to the opposite side. Stand at vertex A and drop a line straight down (at 90°) to side BC — that perpendicular segment is the altitude from A. Every triangle has three altitudes, one from each vertex. The altitude is the 'height' of the triangle when the opposite side is the 'base' — which is why the area of a triangle is ½ × base × height. To construct it, you make a perpendicular from the vertex to the opposite side using compass-and-ruler perpendicular construction.
explanations.textbook: An altitude of a triangle is the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side. Each triangle has three altitudes (one per vertex). The length of an altitude is the height corresponding to the chosen base, used in the area formula Area = ½ × base × height. For obtuse triangles, an altitude may meet the extension of the opposite side outside the triangle.
explanations.expert: The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent at the orthocentre. An altitude is the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side's supporting line; its foot is the orthogonal projection of the vertex onto that line. Altitude length h_a relates to area S by S = ½ a·h_a, so h_a = 2S/a — the basis of the area formula and of many metric relations in triangle geometry.

concepts.reasoning: The altitude is how 'tall' the triangle stands above a chosen base. Measuring height means measuring straight up at a right angle to the base — so the altitude is the perpendicular from the opposite vertex to that base.

useCases.title: Area of a triangular plot
useCases.description: Area = ½ × base × height needs the altitude (height) perpendicular to the base.

useCases.title: Roof pitch
useCases.description: The altitude of a triangular roof cross-section is its peak height above the span.

useCases.title: Triangle height in design
useCases.description: Designers use the altitude to centre text or motifs inside a triangular logo.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The three altitudes of any triangle always meet at a single point — the orthocentre — one of several remarkable 'centres' a triangle has (along with the centroid, incentre, and circumcentre). That three lines defined separately always pass through one point is a beautiful, non-obvious fact discovered by the ancient Greeks.
concepts.mnemonic: Altitude = perpendicular drop from a vertex to the opposite side. It's the triangle's height.
concepts.predictQuestion: What is an altitude of a triangle, and how would you construct the altitude from vertex A to side BC?
whyChain: An altitude measures how tall a triangle stands above a chosen base. 'Height' always means measured straight up — at a right angle — to the base. So the altitude from vertex A is the perpendicular segment dropped from A straight down to the opposite side BC.

To construct it, you drop a perpendicular from A to line BC using the standard compass-and-ruler perpendicular construction: the foot of that perpendicular on BC, joined to A, is the altitude. Every triangle has three such altitudes, one from each vertex.

Altitudes matter because they're the 'height' in Area = ½ × base × height — choose any side as base and its altitude gives the matching height. And remarkably, all three altitudes of any triangle pass through a single point, the orthocentre — one of the elegant hidden 'centres' the Greeks discovered lurking in every triangle.

questions.prompt: Describe the compass steps to construct ∆ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm.
questions.answer: Draw AB = 4 cm; from A draw an arc of radius 5 cm; from B draw an arc of radius 6 cm; their intersection is C; join AC and BC.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Draw the base AB = 4 cm.
Step 2: From A, draw an arc of radius 5 cm (all points 5 cm from A).
Step 3: From B, draw an arc of radius 6 cm crossing the first arc.
Step 4: The intersection is C (exactly 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B). Join AC and BC.
commonMistakes: Swinging the arcs with the wrong radii (mixing up which side goes where).
Forgetting that the arcs only meet if the triangle inequality holds.

variations.prompt: Why is the arc-intersection the correct vertex?
variations.answer: Because it is simultaneously 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B, the required distances.
solutionSteps: Each arc is the set of points at a fixed distance from its centre.

variations.prompt: Construct an equilateral triangle of side 4 cm — what radius for both arcs?
solutionSteps: All sides equal, so both arcs use radius 4 cm.

questions.prompt: What is an altitude of a triangle, and how is it related to the triangle's area?
questions.answer: An altitude is the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the opposite side; it is the height in Area = ½ × base × height.
solutionSteps: An altitude drops perpendicularly from a vertex to the opposite side.
Taking that side as the base, the altitude is the corresponding height.
Area of the triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × base × altitude.
commonMistakes: Confusing the altitude with a side of the triangle.
Forgetting the ½ in the area formula.

variations.prompt: How many altitudes does a triangle have?
solutionSteps: Each vertex has a perpendicular to its opposite side.

variations.prompt: Area of a triangle with base 10 cm and altitude 6 cm?

topics.title: Types of Triangles
topics.summary: Triangles are sorted two ways. By sides: equilateral (all three equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (all different). By angles: acute (all angles < 90°), right (one 90° angle), obtuse (one angle > 90°). A triangle has a name in each system.

concepts.title: Classifying triangles by sides and by angles

explanations.oneLine: By sides: equilateral (3 equal), isosceles (2 equal), scalene (all different). By angles: acute (all < 90°), right (one = 90°), obtuse (one > 90°).
explanations.kidFriendly: Triangles come in families, sorted two different ways. By their SIDES: equilateral has all three sides equal, isosceles has exactly two equal, scalene has all three different. By their ANGLES: acute has all three angles less than 90°, right has exactly one 90° angle, obtuse has one angle bigger than 90°. Note the angle rule is about ALL angles for 'acute' — you can't call a triangle acute just because it has one acute angle (every triangle has at least two!). A triangle gets a name in each system, e.g. 'a right isosceles triangle'.
explanations.textbook: Triangles are classified by side lengths — equilateral (all three sides equal), isosceles (at least two equal), scalene (all three unequal) — and independently by angle measures — acute (all three angles less than 90°), right (exactly one angle of 90°), obtuse (one angle greater than 90°). A triangle can be at most one type in each scheme; an acute triangle requires ALL angles acute, since every triangle already has at least two acute angles.
explanations.expert: The two classifications partition the space of triangle shapes along orthogonal axes (side-equality structure and angle-magnitude structure). They are linked: equilateral ⟹ equiangular (all 60°), hence acute; a right or obtuse triangle cannot be equilateral. The full relationship between side-equality and angle-equality (e.g., isosceles ⟺ two equal base angles) is the subject of later congruence theory.

concepts.reasoning: There are two independent things you can compare: how the sides relate (equal or not) and how big the angles are (under, at, or over 90°). Each gives a way to sort triangles, so every triangle has one label from each scheme.

useCases.title: Set squares
useCases.description: The two drafting set-squares are right triangles: one 45-45-90 (isosceles right), one 30-60-90 (scalene right).

useCases.title: Yield sign
useCases.description: A traffic yield sign is an equilateral (and therefore acute, all-60°) triangle.

useCases.title: Roof gables
useCases.description: Many roof gables are isosceles triangles — two equal slopes meeting at a peak.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The classifications connect deeply: an equilateral triangle is automatically equiangular (all angles 60°) and therefore acute — one shape, names in both systems. The link between equal sides and equal angles (isosceles triangles have equal 'base angles') is one of the oldest theorems in geometry, called the 'pons asinorum' (bridge of asses) in Euclid.
concepts.mnemonic: Two rulers: SIDES (equilateral/isosceles/scalene) and ANGLES (acute/right/obtuse). Every triangle gets one label from each.
concepts.predictQuestion: What is the difference between classifying a triangle by its sides and by its angles, and why can't 'acute' mean 'has one acute angle'?
whyChain: There are two independent features of a triangle you can sort by. One is the SIDES: are all three equal (equilateral), exactly two equal (isosceles), or all different (scalene)? The other is the ANGLES: are all under 90° (acute), is one exactly 90° (right), or is one over 90° (obtuse)? Each scheme gives every triangle a label.

The schemes are independent, so a triangle has a name in each — 'right scalene', 'acute isosceles', and so on. They also interlock: an equilateral triangle has all angles 60°, so it's automatically acute; a right or obtuse triangle can never be equilateral.

The 'acute' definition is subtle: it requires ALL THREE angles to be acute, not just one. Why? Because EVERY triangle has at least two acute angles already (a triangle can have at most one angle that is right or obtuse). So 'has an acute angle' would describe every triangle and tell you nothing — only 'all three acute' carves out a meaningful class.

questions.prompt: Classify a triangle with sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm by its sides. Classify a triangle with angles 40°, 60°, 80° by its angles.
questions.answer: The 5-5-8 triangle is isosceles (two equal sides). The 40-60-80 triangle is acute (all angles < 90°).
solutionSteps: 40°, 60°, 80°: all three angles are less than 90° → acute.
commonMistakes: Calling 5-5-8 equilateral (only two sides are equal, not all three).
Calling the 40-60-80 triangle right or obtuse (none of its angles reaches 90°).

variations.prompt: Classify a triangle with a 90° angle.

questions.prompt: Why must every triangle have at least two acute angles?
questions.answer: Because a triangle can have at most one angle that is 90° or more — two such angles would already total 180° or more, leaving nothing for the third angle. So at least two angles must be acute.
solutionSteps: The three angles of a triangle sum to 180°.
If two angles were each 90° or more, their sum alone would be ≥ 180°, leaving 0° or less for the third — impossible.
So at most one angle can be right or obtuse; the other two must be acute.
Hence every triangle has at least two acute angles.
commonMistakes: Thinking a triangle could have two right angles.
Forgetting the angle-sum is exactly 180°.

variations.prompt: Can a triangle have two obtuse angles?
variations.answer: No — two angles over 90° would exceed 180° on their own.

variations.prompt: Can a triangle be both right-angled and obtuse?
variations.answer: No — that would need two angles ≥ 90°, impossible.
solutionSteps: At most one angle can reach or exceed 90°.

mnemonics.unpacking: A triangle exists only if the two shortest sides together are longer than the longest side (the triangle inequality).
mnemonics.context: Use to test whether three lengths can form a triangle.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Any three lengths can form a triangle.
misconceptions.actually: Only if the sum of every two exceeds the third (triangle inequality). 10, 15, 30 cannot, since 10+15 < 30.

misconceptions.kidsThink: An altitude is one of the sides of the triangle.
misconceptions.actually: An altitude is the PERPENDICULAR from a vertex to the opposite side — usually not a side itself (except in a right triangle).

misconceptions.kidsThink: A triangle is acute if it has an acute angle.
misconceptions.actually: Every triangle has at least two acute angles. 'Acute' means ALL THREE angles are under 90°.

misconceptions.kidsThink: A triangle can have two right angles.
misconceptions.actually: Impossible — two 90° angles already total 180°, leaving nothing for the third. At most one angle can be 90° or more.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Three points always make a triangle.
misconceptions.actually: Three points that lie on one straight line (collinear) do NOT form a triangle — the sides flatten and enclose no area.

realWorldExamples.title: Why bridges are full of triangles
realWorldExamples.body: A triangle is the only polygon that can't flex: fix its three sides and the shape is locked. A four-sided frame can collapse into a slanted parallelogram, but a triangle holds firm. That's why bridges, cranes, electricity pylons and roof trusses are packed with triangles — the triangle inequality and rigidity together make them the strongest simple shape.

realWorldExamples.title: The two set-squares
realWorldExamples.body: Every geometry box has two set-squares: a 45-45-90 (isosceles right triangle) and a 30-60-90 (scalene right triangle). They're shaped to give exactly those angles for drawing — a direct everyday use of triangle classification by both sides and angles.

realWorldExamples.title: Shortest path is a straight line
realWorldExamples.body: When you cut across a park instead of walking two sides of it, you're using the triangle inequality: the direct side is shorter than the detour through a corner. This same rule defines 'distance' in everything from maps to the abstract spaces used in artificial intelligence.

ncertQA.question: What are the vertices, sides and angles of triangle ∆ABC?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Vertices: the corner points A, B, C. Sides: the segments AB, BC, CA joining them. Angles: ∠A, ∠B, ∠C (i.e. ∠CAB, ∠ABC, ∠BCA) at the vertices.

ncertQA.question: Does the set of lengths 10, 15, 30 satisfy the triangle inequality?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: No. 10 + 15 = 25, which is less than 30, so the sum of the two shorter sides does not exceed the longest. The inequality fails and no triangle can be formed.

ncertQA.question: State the triangle inequality and give one example that satisfies it and one that does not.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: The sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the third side. 3, 4, 5 satisfies it (3+4>5, etc.). 10, 15, 30 does not (10+15 < 30).

ncertQA.question: Describe the construction of ∆ABC given AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Draw base AB = 4 cm. From A, draw an arc of radius 5 cm. From B, draw an arc of radius 6 cm intersecting the first. The intersection point is C (it is 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B). Join AC and BC.

ncertQA.question: What is an altitude of a triangle?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: An altitude is the perpendicular segment drawn from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension). It is the triangle's height relative to that side, and there are three altitudes, one from each vertex.

ncertQA.question: Name the three types of triangle classified by sides, and by angles.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: By sides: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (all different). By angles: acute (all angles < 90°), right (one 90° angle), obtuse (one angle > 90°).

ncertQA.question: Why can an acute triangle not be defined as a triangle with one acute angle?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Because every triangle already has at least two acute angles (at most one angle can be 90° or more). So 'has one acute angle' is true of all triangles. An acute triangle is defined as having ALL three angles acute.

ncertQA.question: Two sides of a triangle are 8 cm and 5 cm. What are the possible lengths of the third side?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: The third side must be greater than 8 − 5 = 3 cm and less than 8 + 5 = 13 cm. So 3 cm < third side < 13 cm.

miniProjects.title: Triangle or Not? The Straw Test
steps: For each set, predict using the triangle inequality whether a triangle can be made (do the two shortest beat the longest?).
Now actually try to join each set end-to-end into a triangle.
Record which sets close into a triangle and which collapse flat or won't meet.
For the ones that work, classify each triangle by sides (equilateral / isosceles / scalene).
miniProjects.expectedObservation: The sets that satisfy the triangle inequality ({3,4,5}, {6,6,6}, {7,8,9}) close into triangles; {10,15,30} and {2,2,5} fail because the two short sides can't span the long one — matching your predictions exactly.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: A triangle closes only when the two shorter sides, swung from the ends of the longest, can reach each other — which is precisely the triangle inequality. The straws make the abstract rule physical: too-short sides simply can't meet.

chapters.title: Working with Fractions
chapters.summary: Aaron's tortoise walks 1/4 km an hour — how far in 3 hours? This chapter handles multiplication and division of fractions. Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is repeated addition; multiplying a fraction by a fraction means taking a part 'of' a part (numerators times numerators, denominators times denominators); and dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal — which is why dividing by a number less than 1 makes the answer bigger.

topics.title: Multiplying a Fraction by a Whole Number
topics.summary: 3 × 1/4 is just 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4 — repeated addition, exactly as with whole numbers. To multiply a whole number by a fraction, multiply the whole number by the numerator and keep the denominator.

concepts.title: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number

explanations.oneLine: A whole number times a fraction is repeated addition: 3 × 1/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Multiply the whole number by the numerator, keep the denominator.
explanations.kidFriendly: Aaron's tortoise walks 1/4 km in one hour. How far in 3 hours? Just like 5 × 3 means 3+3+3+3+3, here 3 × 1/4 means 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4 km. Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is repeated addition — nothing new! The shortcut: multiply the whole number by the numerator and leave the denominator alone. So 3 × 1/4 = 3/4; 7 × 3/5 = 21/5 (which is 4 1/5 as a mixed number). The denominator (the size of each piece) doesn't change — you're just counting more of the same-sized pieces.
explanations.textbook: Multiplying a whole number by a fraction is repeated addition of the fraction: n × (a/b) = (a/b) + … (n times) = (n×a)/b. The whole number multiplies the numerator while the denominator is unchanged, since the piece size (1/b) stays fixed and only the count of pieces increases. The result may be converted to a mixed number when improper.
explanations.expert: Scalar multiplication of a rational by a natural number is iterated addition in the additive group of ℚ: n·(a/b) = (na)/b. The denominator is invariant because it indexes the unit fraction 1/b being accumulated; only the multiplicity (numerator) scales. This is the b-fold-refined number line with step 1/b, traversed n×a steps.

concepts.reasoning: Each hour adds another 1/4 km. Three hours stacks three quarter-kilometres: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The pieces are all the same size (quarters), so you just count how many — three — giving 3/4. The denominator names the piece size and stays put.

useCases.title: Tortoise distance
useCases.description: 1/4 km per hour × 3 hours = 3/4 km.

useCases.title: Milk per day
useCases.description: 1/2 glass a day × 7 days = 7/2 = 3½ glasses a week.

useCases.title: Recipe scaling
useCases.description: 3/5 cup per batch × 4 batches = 12/5 = 2 2/5 cups.

concepts.beyondTheBook: This 'multiply the numerator, keep the denominator' rule is the foundation for the harder fraction×fraction rule next. It also explains improper fractions naturally: 7 × 3/5 = 21/5 is more than a whole because you've stacked 21 fifths, and 5 fifths make 1.
concepts.mnemonic: Whole × fraction: multiply the top, keep the bottom. It's just repeated addition.
concepts.predictQuestion: Aaron's tortoise walks 1/4 km each hour. How far does it walk in 3 hours, and why doesn't the denominator change?
whyChain: Multiplying by a whole number is repeated addition — that's true for fractions too. Three hours at 1/4 km each is 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4, three quarter-kilometres stacked together.

All the pieces are the same size: quarters. Adding them just counts how many quarters you have — three — giving 3/4. The denominator (4) names the SIZE of each piece, and that size never changes; only the COUNT (the numerator) grows. So the rule is: multiply the whole number by the numerator, keep the denominator.

This naturally produces improper fractions when the count passes a whole: 7 × 3/5 = 21/5, because you've stacked 21 fifths and every 5 fifths make a whole (= 4 1/5). Understanding 'multiply the top, keep the bottom' as counting same-sized pieces is the launchpad for the trickier fraction-times-fraction rule that follows.

questions.prompt: Aaron's tortoise walks 1/4 km per hour. How far does it walk in 3 hours?
questions.answer: 3/4 km
commonMistakes: Multiplying the denominator too: 3/12 (wrong — the piece size doesn't change).
Adding 3 + 1/4 instead of multiplying.

variations.prompt: Tenzin drinks 1/2 glass of milk daily. How much in a week?

questions.prompt: Multiply 7 × 3/5 and write the answer as a mixed number.
solutionSteps: Multiply the whole number by the numerator: 7 × 3 = 21. Keep denominator 5 → 21/5.
commonMistakes: Multiplying 7 by both 3 and 5.
Forgetting to convert the improper fraction to a mixed number when asked.

topics.title: Multiplying a Fraction by a Fraction
topics.summary: Half OF a third is a sixth: 'of' means multiply. To multiply two fractions, multiply the numerators together and the denominators together: (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd. Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes things smaller — a part of a part.

concepts.title: Fraction times fraction — 'of' means multiply

explanations.oneLine: To multiply two fractions, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators: (a/b) × (c/d) = (a×c)/(b×d). The word 'of' means multiply: 1/2 of 1/3 = 1/6.
explanations.kidFriendly: What is half OF a third? Take a chocolate bar, cut it into 3 equal parts (each 1/3), then halve one of those parts. That little piece is 1/6 of the whole bar. So 1/2 of 1/3 = 1/6 — and 'of' means multiply! The rule: multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms. (1/2) × (1/3) = (1×1)/(2×3) = 1/6. For (2/3) × (4/5) = (2×4)/(3×5) = 8/15. Notice: multiplying by a fraction LESS than 1 makes the result SMALLER — because you're taking only a PART of something.
explanations.textbook: The product of two fractions is (a/b)×(c/d) = (a·c)/(b·d): numerators multiply to give the numerator, denominators multiply to give the denominator. The operator 'of' denotes multiplication (a fraction of a quantity). Multiplying by a proper fraction (value < 1) yields a result smaller than the multiplicand, since one takes a part of it.
explanations.expert: Fraction multiplication is multiplication in the field ℚ: (a/b)(c/d) = ac/bd, well-defined on equivalence classes of integer pairs. Geometrically (a/b)×(c/d) is the area of an (a/b)×(c/d) sub-rectangle of the unit square, partitioned into b·d congruent cells of which a·c are shaded. Multiplication by a value in (0,1) is a contraction, explaining why the product shrinks.

concepts.reasoning: Taking a fraction OF something means cutting it down to a part. A third of the bar, then half of THAT, is a smaller piece still — one of six equal pieces of the whole. Counting the grid of pieces (b across, d down) gives b×d small cells, and you keep a×c of them.

useCases.title: Half of a third of a cake
useCases.description: Cutting a third of a cake in half gives 1/6 of the whole cake.

useCases.title: Discount on a discount
useCases.description: 3/4 of a 1/2-price item costs 3/8 of the original.

useCases.title: Area of a strip
useCases.description: A 2/3 m by 4/5 m mat has area 8/15 m².

concepts.beyondTheBook: The 'of means multiply' rule unlocks percentages (next chapter): '20% of 150' is just (20/100) × 150. It's also the reason multiplication doesn't always 'make bigger' — a fact that surprises many students. Multiplying by a fraction below 1 shrinks; only multiplying by something above 1 grows.
concepts.mnemonic: 'Of' = multiply. Tops × tops, bottoms × bottoms. A part of a part is smaller.
concepts.predictQuestion: What is 1/2 of 1/3 — and does multiplying by 1/2 make the answer bigger or smaller?
whyChain: The word 'of' in maths means multiply. '1/2 of 1/3' is (1/2) × (1/3). Picture a bar cut into three equal thirds, then one third cut in half — that sliver is one of six equal pieces of the whole bar, i.e. 1/6.

The rule that produces this: multiply the numerators (1×1 = 1) and multiply the denominators (2×3 = 6), giving 1/6. For any two fractions, (a/b) × (c/d) = (a×c)/(b×d). The grid picture explains why: splitting into b parts one way and d parts the other makes b×d little cells, and you keep a×c of them.

Crucially, the answer 1/6 is SMALLER than 1/3 — because taking 'half OF' something gives less than you started with. Multiplying by a fraction below 1 always shrinks. This overturns the early intuition that 'multiplying makes bigger', and it's exactly the mechanism behind percentages: '20% of 150' is just (20/100) × 150.

concepts.title: Multiplying and dividing mixed numbers

explanations.oneLine: To multiply or divide mixed numbers, first convert each to an improper fraction, then apply the usual fraction rules.
explanations.kidFriendly: A mixed number like 2½ is part-whole, part-fraction — awkward to multiply directly. The trick: turn it into an improper fraction first. 2½ = (2×2 + 1)/2 = 5/2. So 2½ × 1⅓ becomes 5/2 × 4/3 = 20/6 = 10/3 = 3⅓. For division, convert both and then multiply by the reciprocal. The golden rule for ANY mixed-number multiplication or division: convert to improper fractions FIRST, then it's just the fraction rules you already know. Never multiply the whole parts and fraction parts separately — that gives the wrong answer.
explanations.textbook: A mixed number is converted to an improper fraction by multiplying the whole-number part by the denominator and adding the numerator, keeping the same denominator: a b/c = (a×c + b)/c. Once both factors are improper fractions, multiplication and division proceed by the standard rules (multiply numerators and denominators; for division, multiply by the reciprocal). For example, 2½ × 1⅓ = 5/2 × 4/3 = 20/6 = 10/3 = 3⅓.
explanations.expert: Mixed-number notation a b/c denotes a + b/c, a sum, not a product — which is exactly why naive part-wise multiplication fails (it ignores the cross terms of (a + b/c)(d + e/f)). Converting to a single improper fraction collapses the sum into one rational p/q, after which the field operations of ℚ apply directly. This is a worked instance of normalising to a canonical form before computing.

concepts.reasoning: A mixed number is secretly an addition (2½ means 2 + ½), and you can't multiply two sums by just multiplying their matching parts. Rewriting each mixed number as a single improper fraction turns it into one number, so the ordinary multiply/divide rules apply cleanly.

useCases.title: Scaling a recipe
useCases.description: 1½ cups of rice × 2½ batches = 3/2 × 5/2 = 15/4 = 3¾ cups.

useCases.title: Cloth lengths
useCases.description: 2¼ m of cloth for each of 1⅓ curtains needs 9/4 × 4/3 = 3 m.

useCases.title: Sharing land
useCases.description: A 4½-acre plot split into ¾-acre shares: 9/2 ÷ 3/4 = 9/2 × 4/3 = 6 shares.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Calculators and computers store mixed numbers internally as single fractions (or decimals) for exactly this reason — a sum-form like 2½ is ambiguous to operate on until normalised. The habit of converting to a canonical single value before computing recurs throughout algebra (improper fractions, single powers, combined logarithms).
concepts.mnemonic: Mixed number? Make it improper FIRST. (whole × denominator + numerator) over the denominator.
concepts.predictQuestion: How would you compute 2½ × 1⅓ — and why can't you just multiply the whole parts and the fraction parts separately?
whyChain: A mixed number is really a hidden addition: 2½ means 2 + ½, not 2 times ½. That single fact is the root of every mixed-number mistake — you can't multiply two sums by pairing up their matching pieces, because that drops the cross-terms.

So we normalise first: convert each mixed number to a single improper fraction using (whole × denominator + numerator) over the denominator. 2½ becomes 5/2; 1⅓ becomes 4/3. Now each is ONE number, not a sum, and the ordinary fraction rules apply without any cross-term trouble.

From there it's the rules you already know: multiply numerators and denominators (5/2 × 4/3 = 20/6 = 10/3 = 3⅓), or for division multiply by the reciprocal. Convert back to a mixed number at the end if you like. 'Make it improper first' is a specific case of a deep habit — put a quantity in a single canonical form before operating on it, a move you'll use throughout algebra.

questions.prompt: Find 1/2 of 1/3.
commonMistakes: Adding the fractions instead of multiplying.
Multiplying tops and adding bottoms.

questions.prompt: A shop offers 3/4 of the price on an item already at 1/2 price. What fraction of the ORIGINAL price do you pay?
questions.answer: 3/8 of the original price.
commonMistakes: Adding 3/4 + 1/2 instead of multiplying.
Thinking the answer is bigger than 1/2 (taking 3/4 OF it makes it smaller).

solutionSteps: Multiplying by a fraction < 1 shrinks the value.

questions.prompt: Compute 2½ × 1⅓ by converting to improper fractions first.
commonMistakes: Multiplying whole parts and fraction parts separately (2×1 and ½×⅓) — wrong, because a mixed number is a sum.
Forgetting to convert to improper fractions before multiplying.

questions.prompt: A 4½-acre plot is divided into ¾-acre shares. How many shares are there?
questions.answer: 6 shares
commonMistakes: Dividing 4½ by ¾ without converting to improper fractions.
Multiplying instead of dividing (the question asks how many shares fit).

variations.prompt: How many ½-cup servings are in 3½ cups?
How many ⅔-m pieces from 4 m?

topics.title: Division of Fractions
topics.summary: Dividing means asking 'what times the divisor gives the dividend?'. For fractions, dividing by a/b is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal b/a. So 1 ÷ 2/3 = 1 × 3/2 = 3/2. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a BIGGER answer.

concepts.title: Dividing by a fraction — multiply by the reciprocal

explanations.oneLine: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal (flip it): a ÷ (c/d) = a × (d/c). Dividing by a number less than 1 makes the answer larger.
explanations.kidFriendly: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 because 4 × 3 = 12. Division asks 'what times the divisor gives the dividend?'. Same for fractions. What is 1 ÷ 2/3? We need '2/3 × ? = 1'. The answer is 3/2, because (2/3) × (3/2) = 1 — the 2s and 3s cancel. So dividing by 2/3 is the same as MULTIPLYING by its reciprocal 3/2 (just flip the fraction). Rule: to divide by a fraction, flip it and multiply. And here's the surprise: 1 ÷ 2/3 = 3/2 is BIGGER than 1 — dividing by a number less than 1 grows the result, because you're asking 'how many two-thirds fit into 1?' and more than one does.
explanations.textbook: Division by a fraction equals multiplication by its reciprocal: a ÷ (c/d) = a × (d/c). This follows because division is the inverse of multiplication: a ÷ (c/d) is the number that, multiplied by c/d, gives a, namely a·(d/c). The reciprocal of c/d is d/c (their product is 1). Dividing by a proper fraction (< 1) yields a quotient larger than the dividend.
explanations.expert: In the field ℚ, division is multiplication by the multiplicative inverse: a/(c/d) = a·(c/d)⁻¹ = a·(d/c), where (c/d)⁻¹ = d/c since (c/d)(d/c) = 1. Division by an element of (0,1) is multiplication by its inverse in (1,∞), hence an expansion. The 'invert and multiply' rule is precisely the existence of multiplicative inverses for all nonzero rationals.

concepts.reasoning: Division undoes multiplication. 'a ÷ (c/d)' asks which number times c/d gives a. Since (c/d) × (d/c) = 1, multiplying a by the flipped fraction d/c lands you exactly there. And because fitting small pieces (less than 1) into a quantity takes many of them, the count comes out large.

useCases.title: Sharing oil
useCases.description: 5 litres shared so each gets 1/3 litre: 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15 portions.

useCases.title: Cutting ribbon
useCases.description: How many 1/4 m pieces from 2 m? 2 ÷ 1/4 = 8 pieces.

useCases.title: Cooking servings
useCases.description: 3 cups of rice in 1/2-cup servings: 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 servings.

concepts.beyondTheBook: 'Dividing makes smaller' is another early intuition this chapter overturns: 2 ÷ 1/4 = 8 is much bigger than 2, because you're counting how many quarter-pieces fit. Together with 'multiplying can make smaller', fractions force a more honest understanding of what multiplication and division really mean.
concepts.mnemonic: To divide by a fraction, flip it and multiply. Dividing by < 1 makes BIGGER.
concepts.predictQuestion: What is 1 ÷ 2/3, and why is the answer bigger than 1?
whyChain: Division asks: what number times the divisor gives the dividend? '1 ÷ 2/3' asks '2/3 times what equals 1?'. The answer is 3/2, because (2/3) × (3/2) = 1 — the 2s and 3s cancel. So dividing by 2/3 is the same as multiplying by its flipped form, the reciprocal 3/2.

That's the general rule: to divide by a fraction, flip it (swap numerator and denominator) and multiply. It works because a fraction times its reciprocal is 1, so multiplying by the reciprocal exactly undoes the divisor — which is what division means.

The answer 3/2 is BIGGER than the 1 we started with, which feels strange until you read the division as 'how many two-thirds fit into 1?' — and one-and-a-half of them do. Dividing by any number less than 1 makes the result larger. This (with 'multiplying by a fraction shrinks') replaces the naive 'multiply-bigger, divide-smaller' rule with what those operations truly do.

questions.prompt: Compute 1 ÷ 2/3 by multiplying by the reciprocal.
solutionSteps: Dividing by 2/3 = multiplying by its reciprocal 3/2.
commonMistakes: Flipping the dividend instead of the divisor.
Multiplying by 2/3 instead of its reciprocal.

questions.prompt: How many 1/2-cup servings can be made from 3 cups of rice? Does the answer being bigger than 3 make sense?
questions.answer: 6 servings. Yes — dividing by a number less than 1 (1/2) gives a result bigger than the dividend, because many small servings fit into 3 cups.
solutionSteps: Six half-cup servings fit into 3 cups.
Bigger than 3 makes sense: each serving is small, so there are more of them than there are whole cups.
commonMistakes: Computing 3 × 1/2 = 1.5 (multiplying instead of dividing).
Expecting the answer to be smaller than 3.

glossary.definition: A number written a/b representing a parts out of b equal parts of a whole.
The top number of a fraction; how many parts are taken.
The bottom number of a fraction; how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
In fraction problems, 'of' means multiply.
A fraction whose numerator is greater than or equal to its denominator.
A whole number together with a proper fraction.
The fraction obtained by swapping numerator and denominator; a number times its reciprocal is 1.
In a ÷ b = c, a is the dividend, b the divisor, c the quotient.
A fraction less than 1 (numerator smaller than denominator).
The result of multiplying fractions: tops multiply, bottoms multiply.

mnemonics.unpacking: Whole × fraction: multiply the numerator by the whole number, keep the denominator (3 × 1/4 = 3/4).
mnemonics.context: Use for whole-number times a fraction.

mnemonics.unpacking: In fraction problems, 'of' means multiply: tops × tops, bottoms × bottoms.
mnemonics.context: Use for a fraction of a fraction (or of a quantity).

mnemonics.unpacking: To divide by a fraction, flip it to its reciprocal and multiply: 1 ÷ 2/3 = 1 × 3/2.
mnemonics.context: Use for dividing by a fraction.

misconceptions.kidsThink: To multiply a whole number by a fraction, multiply both the numerator and denominator.
misconceptions.actually: Only multiply the numerator; keep the denominator. 3 × 1/4 = 3/4, not 3/12. The piece size doesn't change.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Multiplying always makes a number bigger.
misconceptions.actually: Multiplying by a fraction LESS than 1 makes it smaller. 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6, smaller than both.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Dividing always makes a number smaller.
misconceptions.actually: Dividing by a number less than 1 makes it BIGGER. 2 ÷ 1/4 = 8, because eight quarter-pieces fit in 2.

misconceptions.kidsThink: To divide by a fraction, flip the first fraction (the dividend).
misconceptions.actually: You flip the DIVISOR (the one you're dividing BY) and multiply: 1 ÷ 2/3 = 1 × 3/2.

misconceptions.kidsThink: 'Half of a third' means 1/2 + 1/3.
misconceptions.actually: 'Of' means multiply: 1/2 of 1/3 = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6, not 1/2 + 1/3.

realWorldExamples.title: Sharing oil among families
realWorldExamples.body: Manju and two neighbours share 5 litres of oil equally among 3 families: each gets 5 ÷ 3 = 5/3 litres a week. Over 4 weeks one family gets 4 × 5/3 = 20/3 = 6 2/3 litres. Real sharing problems are fraction multiplication and division in disguise.

realWorldExamples.title: Discount on a discount
realWorldExamples.body: A jacket at half price, with a further 'pay 3/4' festive offer, costs 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8 of the original. Shoppers who think the discounts 'add up' are surprised — fractions of fractions multiply, and the result is a smaller fraction of the original.

realWorldExamples.title: How many servings?
realWorldExamples.body: A cook with 3 cups of batter making 1/2-cup idlis gets 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 idlis. Dividing by a small fraction gives a big count — the everyday meaning of 'how many small pieces fit'.

miniProjects.title: Chocolate-Bar Fraction Lab
needs: A bar of chocolate or a sheet of paper marked in a grid
steps: Take one whole bar (or paper rectangle). Cut/mark it into 3 equal parts — each is 1/3.
Now halve ONE of those thirds. What fraction of the whole is that small piece? Confirm it is 1/6.
Write the multiplication: 1/2 of 1/3 = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.
Now take a whole bar and see how many 1/4-pieces it gives: that's 1 ÷ 1/4 = 4.
Predict, then check: how many 1/2-pieces are in 3 bars? (3 ÷ 1/2 = 6.)
miniProjects.expectedObservation: Taking a part OF a part gives a smaller piece (multiplying by a fraction < 1 shrinks), while cutting a whole into small pieces gives MANY of them (dividing by a fraction < 1 grows the count).
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Multiplying fractions partitions the whole into a grid of (bottom×bottom) pieces and keeps (top×top) of them — a part of a part. Dividing asks how many divisor-pieces fit into the dividend, so small pieces yield a large count. The chocolate makes both rules tangible.

chapters.title: Geometric Twins
chapters.summary: How do you recreate a figure exactly without tracing it? You measure just enough to pin it down. Two figures that are exact copies — same shape AND same size — are congruent. This chapter finds the minimum measurements that force two triangles to be congruent (the SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS criteria) and uses congruence to prove that a triangle's equal sides face equal angles.

topics.title: Geometric Twins & Congruence
topics.summary: Two figures are congruent if one can be placed exactly on top of the other — same shape and size. Knowing which measurements pin a figure down matters: all three sides of a triangle fix it completely, but two sides alone leave two possible triangles.

concepts.title: Congruent figures — exact copies

explanations.oneLine: Two figures are congruent (written ≅) if one can be moved to fit exactly on top of the other — they have the same shape and the same size.
explanations.kidFriendly: To recreate a signboard symbol on another board, you don't need to trace it — you can MEASURE it and rebuild it. Two figures that come out exactly the same — same shape, same size — are called congruent, written with the symbol ≅. If you could slide, turn or flip one to land perfectly on the other, they're congruent. A photocopy at 100% is congruent to the original; a photocopy enlarged to 150% is the same SHAPE but not congruent (wrong size). Congruence is about being a perfect twin, not just a look-alike.
explanations.textbook: Two geometric figures are congruent if there is a rigid motion (translation, rotation, reflection, or a combination) mapping one exactly onto the other; they have identical shape and size. Congruence is denoted ≅. Congruent figures have all corresponding sides and angles equal. Congruence differs from similarity, which preserves shape but allows a change of size.
explanations.expert: Congruence is the equivalence relation induced by the group of isometries of the Euclidean plane (the group generated by translations, rotations and reflections). Two figures are congruent iff some isometry maps one onto the other; since isometries preserve distances and angles, all corresponding measurements are equal. This is the geometric notion of 'sameness up to position and orientation'.

concepts.reasoning: Two shapes are the same in the strongest sense if you could pick one up and lay it perfectly over the other with nothing sticking out or falling short. That requires every length and every angle to match — same shape and same size.

useCases.title: Photocopy at 100%
useCases.description: An exact-size photocopy is congruent to the original; a resized one is not.

useCases.title: Manufactured parts
useCases.description: Identical machine parts must be congruent so they're interchangeable.

useCases.title: Tile twins
useCases.description: Floor tiles cut to the same size and shape are congruent and fit any slot.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Congruence is the foundation of mass manufacturing: every bolt, brick or microchip of a type must be congruent so parts are interchangeable. The distinction between congruent (same size) and merely similar (same shape, different size) becomes hugely important in the next stage of geometry and in map/scale-model work.
concepts.mnemonic: Congruent = perfect twin: same shape AND same size, written ≅.
concepts.predictQuestion: If you make a 150%-enlarged photocopy of a drawing, is the copy congruent to the original? Why or why not?
whyChain: Congruence means one figure can be laid exactly onto the other — every length and every angle matching, nothing over or short. It's 'sameness' in the strongest geometric sense, allowing only sliding, turning or flipping.

A 150% enlargement has the SAME SHAPE as the original but every length is 1.5× bigger. You could never lay it exactly on top — it would overhang on all sides. So it is NOT congruent; it is merely 'similar' (same shape, different size). A 100% copy, by contrast, would match exactly and IS congruent.

This same-size requirement is why congruence underpins manufacturing — interchangeable bolts and bricks must be congruent, not just similar. And the congruent-vs-similar distinction becomes central later: scale models and maps are similar to reality, while a spare part must be congruent to the one it replaces.

concepts.title: Which measurements pin a triangle down

explanations.oneLine: All three side lengths fix a triangle completely (SSS), but two sides alone don't — they leave two different possible triangles.
explanations.kidFriendly: Meera and Rabia want to copy a triangular frame too big to trace. Meera says: just measure the three sides — that's enough to rebuild an exact copy! Is she right? Yes: with all three side lengths (say 4, 6, 8 cm), you draw the base and swing arcs (as in the triangle chapter), and the triangle is fixed. But what if you only knew TWO sides? Drawing a 6 cm base and swinging a 4 cm and 8 cm arc gives TWO intersection points — two different triangles (one above, one below). So two sides aren't enough to pin it down; you need the right THREE pieces of information. Finding the minimum sufficient measurements is the heart of congruence.
explanations.textbook: Three side lengths uniquely determine a triangle up to congruence (the SSS criterion): constructing with the three given lengths yields exactly one triangle shape. Two sides alone are insufficient — the arc construction produces two intersection points (a triangle and its reflection across the base are distinct unless further constrained). Determining minimal sufficient information is the subject of the congruence criteria.
explanations.expert: The question of which data determine a triangle up to congruence is the question of which measurement-tuples have a unique realisation under the isometry group. SSS, SAS, ASA, and RHS are the minimal sufficient sets; SSA is famously NOT sufficient (the 'ambiguous case'), corresponding exactly to the two arc-intersection points. This is the rigidity theory of the triangle.

concepts.reasoning: To copy a shape exactly, you need just enough measurements to leave only one possible figure. Three sides do that for a triangle. Fewer, or the wrong combination, can leave more than one figure consistent with your measurements — so the copy isn't guaranteed.

useCases.title: Copying a frame
useCases.description: Measure all three sides of a triangular frame to rebuild it exactly.

useCases.title: Surveying land
useCases.description: Surveyors fix a triangular plot by measuring sufficient sides/angles to remove ambiguity.

useCases.title: Truss replacement
useCases.description: A replacement truss needs enough measurements (3 sides) to be congruent to the old one.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The discovery that exactly three well-chosen measurements pin down a triangle is the basis of trigonometry and surveying — 'triangulation' lets you map vast distances by measuring a few sides and angles. The 'ambiguous' two-sides case is a famous pitfall that the congruence criteria are designed to avoid.
concepts.mnemonic: Three sides fix a triangle. Two sides leave two possibilities — not enough.
concepts.predictQuestion: Meera says three side lengths are enough to copy a triangle exactly, with no angles needed. Is she right — and would two sides be enough?
whyChain: Copying a figure exactly means taking just enough measurements that only ONE figure fits them. For a triangle, all three side lengths do exactly that: draw the base, swing an arc of each other length from the two ends, and the apex is fixed — one triangle (the SSS criterion).

Two sides alone are NOT enough. Drawing a base and swinging just two arcs gives two intersection points — one above the base, one below — so two different triangles fit the same two-side data. You can't be sure which matches the original.

So Meera is right: three sides suffice, angles unnecessary. The deeper lesson is about MINIMUM sufficient information — exactly three well-chosen measurements pin a triangle down, which is why surveyors can 'triangulate' huge distances from a few measurements, and why the congruence criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) matter: they list precisely the data that leave no ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Are an original drawing and its 150% enlargement congruent? Explain.
questions.answer: No. They have the same shape but different sizes, so the enlargement can't be placed exactly on the original. They are similar, not congruent.
solutionSteps: Congruent means same shape AND same size (one fits exactly on the other).
A 150% enlargement is 1.5× bigger in every length — same shape, bigger size.
It can't lie exactly on the original, so it is NOT congruent (only similar).
commonMistakes: Thinking same shape is enough for congruence (size must match too).
Confusing congruent with similar.

variations.prompt: Is a 100% photocopy congruent to the original?

questions.prompt: Why are two side lengths not enough to copy a triangle exactly, while three are?
questions.answer: Two sides leave two possible triangles (the two arc-intersection points above and below the base). Three sides fix the triangle uniquely (SSS).
solutionSteps: With a base and two given side lengths, arcs from each base end cross at TWO points — giving two different triangles.
So two sides don't determine a unique triangle.
With all three sides, the construction yields exactly one triangle (up to position) — the SSS criterion.
commonMistakes: Assuming any two measurements determine a triangle.
Forgetting the second arc-intersection point.

variations.prompt: Do three sides 4, 6, 8 determine a unique triangle?
How many triangles fit a 6 cm base with 4 cm and 8 cm arcs?

topics.title: Congruence Criteria for Triangles
topics.summary: You don't need all six measurements (3 sides + 3 angles) to guarantee two triangles are congruent. Four shortcuts work: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and the side between them), and RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, one side).

concepts.title: SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS

explanations.oneLine: Two triangles are congruent if they match by SSS (3 sides), SAS (2 sides + included angle), ASA (2 angles + included side), or RHS (right angle + hypotenuse + a side).
explanations.kidFriendly: A triangle has six measurements (3 sides, 3 angles) — but you don't need all six to know two triangles are identical. Four reliable shortcuts: SSS — all three sides equal. SAS — two sides and the angle BETWEEN them equal. ASA — two angles and the side BETWEEN them equal. RHS — for right triangles, the right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal. If any one of these matches, the triangles are congruent (≅), and then ALL their other parts match too. One warning: two sides and a NON-included angle (SSA) does NOT guarantee congruence — that's the ambiguous two-triangle case.
explanations.textbook: Four sufficient congruence criteria for triangles: SSS (three pairs of equal sides), SAS (two pairs of equal sides with the included angle equal), ASA (two pairs of equal angles with the included side equal), and RHS (in right triangles, equal hypotenuse and one equal leg). Each guarantees all remaining corresponding parts are equal (CPCT). SSA is not a valid criterion (ambiguous case).
explanations.expert: The congruence criteria are the minimal determining data sets under the planar isometry group. SSS, SAS, ASA (and AAS, RHS as derived cases) each fix the triangle up to isometry; their sufficiency is provable from the parallel postulate and the rigid-motion axioms. SSA fails because the side-side-angle data can correspond to two non-congruent triangles (the law-of-sines ambiguity), matching the two arc intersections.

concepts.reasoning: Each criterion gives just enough to remove all freedom. Fix three sides, or two sides and their corner, or two angles and their shared side, and the triangle can't be anything but one specific shape — so two triangles meeting the criterion must be identical.

useCases.title: Quality control
useCases.description: Checking SAS on manufactured brackets confirms they're all congruent without measuring everything.

useCases.title: Proving figures match
useCases.description: Geometry proofs use SSS/SAS/ASA to establish two triangles are congruent, then conclude their other parts are equal.

useCases.title: Bridge trusses
useCases.description: Engineers rely on congruent triangles (fixed by SSS) for predictable, identical load-bearing units.

concepts.beyondTheBook: These criteria are the toolkit of geometric PROOF. Once you show two triangles are congruent by one criterion, you instantly get all their other equal parts 'for free' (CPCT — corresponding parts of congruent triangles). This proof engine drives most of school geometry, including the isosceles-triangle theorem in the next topic.
concepts.mnemonic: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS each force congruence. SSA does NOT (ambiguous).
concepts.predictQuestion: If two triangles have two sides and the angle BETWEEN those sides equal, are they congruent? Which criterion is that?
whyChain: A triangle has six measurements, but you don't need all six to guarantee two are identical — just enough to remove all freedom. Two sides with the angle BETWEEN them (the included angle) is exactly such a set: fix two arms and the corner between them, and the third side and remaining angles have no choice. That's the SAS criterion, and yes, the triangles are congruent.

There are four such sufficient sets: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides + included angle), ASA (two angles + included side), and RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, one leg). Meeting any one forces congruence, after which ALL remaining parts match automatically (CPCT).

One critical caution: two sides and a NON-included angle (SSA) does NOT work — it can describe two different triangles, the same ambiguity as the two arc-intersection points. That's why the valid criteria specifically require the INCLUDED angle or side. These criteria are the engine of geometric proof: establish congruence by one of them, then harvest every other equal part for free.

questions.prompt: Name the four triangle-congruence criteria and state what each requires.
questions.answer: SSS: three pairs of equal sides. SAS: two equal sides and the equal angle BETWEEN them. ASA: two equal angles and the equal side BETWEEN them. RHS: in right triangles, equal hypotenuse and one equal leg.
solutionSteps: SSS = Side-Side-Side: all three sides equal.
SAS = Side-Angle-Side: two sides and the included angle equal.
ASA = Angle-Side-Angle: two angles and the included side equal.
commonMistakes: Listing SSA as a valid criterion (it isn't — ambiguous).
Forgetting that SAS/ASA need the angle/side to be the INCLUDED one.

variations.prompt: Is SSA a valid congruence criterion?
variations.answer: No — it's the ambiguous case (two possible triangles).

variations.prompt: Two triangles share 3 equal angles. Congruent?
variations.answer: Not necessarily — equal angles give same shape (similar) but maybe different size.

questions.prompt: Two triangles have sides 5 cm and 7 cm with a 60° angle between those two sides in each. Are they congruent? By which criterion?
questions.answer: Yes, by SAS — two sides (5 and 7) and the included angle (60°) match.
solutionSteps: Both triangles share two sides: 5 cm and 7 cm.
The 60° angle is BETWEEN those two sides (included).
Two sides + included angle equal → SAS → the triangles are congruent.
commonMistakes: Calling it SSA because an angle and sides are involved — here the angle is INCLUDED, so it's SAS.
Thinking more measurements are needed.

variations.prompt: Triangles with a 90° angle, equal hypotenuse and one equal leg — congruent by?
Two angles 40°, 60° and the side between them equal — which criterion?

topics.title: Angles of Isosceles & Equilateral Triangles
topics.summary: Congruence proves a beautiful fact: in an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are themselves equal. Drop the altitude from the apex and the two halves are congruent (RHS), forcing the base angles to match. An equilateral triangle therefore has all three angles equal — each 60°.

concepts.title: Equal sides face equal angles; equilateral angles are 60°

explanations.oneLine: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal; in an equilateral triangle all three angles are equal, each 60°.
explanations.kidFriendly: Take an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC. Drop the altitude from A to BC, meeting it at D. Now compare the two halves, ∆ADB and ∆ADC: AB = AC (given), ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90° (altitude), and AD is shared. By RHS, the two halves are congruent! So their matching angles ∠B and ∠C must be equal. Conclusion: the angles OPPOSITE the equal sides are equal — equal sides face equal angles. For an equilateral triangle (all sides equal), all three angles must be equal; since they sum to 180°, each is 180 ÷ 3 = 60°. Congruence turns a 'looks true' into a 'proven true'.
explanations.textbook: Isosceles triangle theorem: if two sides of a triangle are equal, the angles opposite them are equal. Proof: dropping the altitude from the apex creates two triangles congruent by RHS (equal hypotenuses = the equal sides, shared altitude, right angles), so the base angles are equal as corresponding parts. Corollary: an equilateral triangle is equiangular, and since the angles sum to 180°, each equals 60°.
explanations.expert: The isosceles base-angle theorem (Euclid I.5, the pons asinorum) follows from RHS congruence of the two sub-triangles formed by the apex altitude. Its converse (equal base angles imply equal sides) also holds. The equilateral corollary (each angle 60°) uses the angle-sum 180°. These results exhibit congruence as the deductive engine deriving metric properties from defining conditions.

concepts.reasoning: Fold an isosceles triangle along the altitude from its apex: the two halves land exactly on each other (they're congruent), so the two base angles coincide — they must be equal. Equal sides, equal opposite angles. If all three sides are equal, symmetry forces all three angles equal, and three equal angles summing to 180° are 60° each.

useCases.title: Roof gable symmetry
useCases.description: An isosceles roof gable has equal base angles — the two slopes meet the wall at the same angle.

useCases.title: Equilateral signboards
useCases.description: A yield sign (equilateral) has three 60° corners by this theorem.

useCases.title: Folding test
useCases.description: Folding an isosceles cutout along its altitude makes the halves match — congruence you can feel.

concepts.beyondTheBook: This is Euclid's Proposition I.5, nicknamed the 'pons asinorum' (bridge of asses) because it was the first real test of a geometry student's reasoning. Using congruence to PROVE the base angles equal — rather than just measuring them — is a milestone: it's deductive geometry doing what measurement never can, guaranteeing a fact for ALL isosceles triangles at once.
concepts.mnemonic: Equal sides → equal opposite angles (prove via altitude + RHS). Equilateral → all 60°.
concepts.predictQuestion: In an isosceles triangle with AB = AC, how can congruence prove that ∠B = ∠C — and what does this make each angle of an equilateral triangle?
whyChain: Drop the altitude from the apex A to the base BC, meeting it at D. Now compare the two halves ∆ADB and ∆ADC: the equal sides give AB = AC, the altitude gives ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°, and AD is shared by both. That's the RHS criterion — so the two halves are congruent.

Congruent triangles have all corresponding parts equal, so ∠B = ∠C. This proves the theorem: the angles opposite the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are equal. It's a genuine proof — true for EVERY isosceles triangle, not just measured in one.

An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, so by the same reasoning all three angles are equal. Since a triangle's angles sum to 180°, each must be 180 ÷ 3 = 60°. This is Euclid's famous 'pons asinorum', and it shows congruence doing what a ruler never could — guaranteeing a fact for all triangles of a type at once.

questions.prompt: In isosceles ∆ABC, AB = AC and ∠A = 80°. Find ∠B and ∠C.
solutionSteps: Angles opposite the equal sides are equal: ∠B = ∠C.
commonMistakes: Assuming ∠B and ∠C are different.
Forgetting the angle-sum of 180°.

variations.prompt: Isosceles with apex angle 40°. Base angles?
Isosceles with each base angle 65°. Apex angle?

questions.prompt: What is each angle of an equilateral triangle, and why?
questions.answer: 60° each, because all three sides are equal so all three angles are equal, and they sum to 180° (180 ÷ 3 = 60).
solutionSteps: All sides equal → all angles equal (equal sides face equal angles).
commonMistakes: Saying 90° (confusing with a right angle or square).
Dividing 360 instead of 180 by 3.

variations.prompt: If a triangle has all angles 60°, must it be equilateral?
variations.answer: Yes — equal angles face equal sides.
