glossary.definition: Having the same shape and size; one figure fits exactly on the other. Symbol ≅.
Same shape but possibly different size (not necessarily congruent).
glossary.example: A photo and its 150% enlargement are similar.

glossary.definition: Two triangles are congruent if all three pairs of sides are equal.
Congruent if two sides and the included angle are equal.
Congruent if two angles and the included side are equal.
For right triangles: congruent if the right angle, hypotenuse and one side match.
glossary.example: Used to split an isosceles triangle.

glossary.definition: The angle between two named sides.
glossary.example: In SAS, the angle between the two given sides.

glossary.definition: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles (are equal) — used after proving congruence.
A triangle with two equal sides; the angles opposite them are equal.
Two sides and a non-included angle do NOT determine a unique triangle.

mnemonics.unpacking: Congruent figures match exactly: equal shape AND equal size. Similar = same shape only.
mnemonics.context: Use to distinguish congruent from similar.

mnemonics.unpacking: The four valid congruence criteria. SSA is the ambiguous case and is NOT valid.
mnemonics.context: Use when proving two triangles congruent.

mnemonics.unpacking: In any triangle, equal sides face equal angles (and vice versa). Equilateral → all 60°.
mnemonics.context: Use for isosceles and equilateral angle problems.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Figures of the same shape are congruent.
misconceptions.actually: They must also be the same SIZE. Same shape but different size means similar, not congruent.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Two sides and any angle prove congruence.
misconceptions.actually: Only if the angle is INCLUDED (between the sides) — that's SAS. A non-included angle (SSA) is ambiguous and does NOT prove congruence.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Three equal angles (AAA) make triangles congruent.
misconceptions.actually: AAA gives the same SHAPE (similar) but the sizes can differ. You need a side too.

misconceptions.kidsThink: The base angles of an isosceles triangle just happen to look equal.
misconceptions.actually: They are PROVABLY equal — dropping the altitude makes two congruent (RHS) halves, forcing the base angles to match.

misconceptions.kidsThink: An equilateral triangle's angles are 90° or 360÷3.
misconceptions.actually: They are 60° each: three equal angles summing to 180° give 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

realWorldExamples.title: Interchangeable parts
realWorldExamples.body: A factory making door hinges must make every hinge congruent to a master design — same shape and same size — so any hinge fits any door. 'Similar but not congruent' (slightly bigger) would jam. Congruence is the silent guarantee behind every interchangeable manufactured part.

realWorldExamples.title: Triangulation in surveying
realWorldExamples.body: Surveyors map huge distances by measuring just enough of a triangle (sides and angles satisfying a congruence criterion) to fix it completely, then chaining triangles across the land. The fact that three well-chosen measurements pin a triangle down is what makes large-scale mapping possible.

realWorldExamples.title: The pons asinorum
realWorldExamples.body: Proving an isosceles triangle's base angles equal — using congruent halves rather than a protractor — is Euclid's Proposition I.5, the historic 'bridge of asses' that tested every geometry beginner. It shows reasoning achieving certainty that measurement alone never can.

ncertQA.question: What does it mean for two figures to be congruent?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: They have the same shape AND the same size, so one can be placed exactly on top of the other (by sliding, turning, or flipping). Congruence is written with the symbol ≅.

ncertQA.question: Meera says the three side lengths are enough to make a triangle congruent to a given one, with no angles needed. Is she right?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Yes. By the SSS criterion, three equal sides determine a triangle uniquely up to congruence. Constructing with the three lengths gives exactly one triangle shape.

ncertQA.question: Why don't two sides alone determine a unique triangle?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Drawing the base and swinging arcs of the two given side-lengths from its ends produces two intersection points (one above and one below the base), giving two different triangles. So two sides are not enough.

ncertQA.question: List the valid congruence criteria for triangles.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA (two angles and the included side), and RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, one side). SSA is NOT a valid criterion.

ncertQA.question: Two triangles have two pairs of equal sides with equal included angles. Are they congruent? By which rule?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Yes, by SAS (Side-Angle-Side). Two sides and the angle between them being equal forces the triangles to be congruent.

ncertQA.question: Prove that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: In ∆ABC with AB = AC, drop the altitude AD to BC. Then AB = AC, ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°, and AD is common, so ∆ADB ≅ ∆ADC by RHS. Hence ∠B = ∠C by CPCT — the angles opposite the equal sides are equal.

ncertQA.question: In isosceles ∆ABC with AB = AC and ∠A = 80°, find ∠B and ∠C.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: ∠B = ∠C (equal sides, equal opposite angles). Their sum is 180 − 80 = 100°, so each is 50°.

ncertQA.question: What are the angles of an equilateral triangle, and why?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Each angle is 60°. All sides are equal, so all angles are equal; three equal angles summing to 180° give 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

miniProjects.title: Congruence by Cut-and-Fold
steps: Draw any triangle and cut it out. Trace around it, then cut a second copy — the two should be congruent.
Stack them: do they match exactly when slid, turned or flipped? If yes, they're congruent.
Now draw an isosceles triangle (two equal sides) and cut it out.
Fold it along the line from the apex to the middle of the base. Do the two halves land exactly on each other?
Mark the two base angles before folding; after folding, check that they coincide — proving they're equal.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: The two cut copies match exactly (congruent). The isosceles triangle's two halves coincide on folding, and its two base angles land on top of each other — showing equal sides really do face equal angles.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Folding the isosceles triangle along the apex altitude maps one half onto the other — a reflection that is a congruence. Because the halves are congruent, the base angles are corresponding parts and must be equal. The scissors-and-fold makes Euclid's proof physical.

chapters.title: Operations with Integers
chapters.summary: A carrom coin struck left or right, tokens dropped into or pulled out of a bag — these models make integer arithmetic concrete. This chapter adds and subtracts integers (same signs add, opposite signs cancel; subtracting is adding the opposite) and multiplies them, deriving the famous sign rules: a positive times a negative is negative, and a negative times a negative is positive.

topics.title: Adding Integers
topics.summary: Model a struck carrom coin moving left (negative) or right (positive). Adding two integers of the SAME sign stacks them (the result keeps that sign); adding OPPOSITE signs cancels — a positive and a negative token form a 'zero pair' that vanishes.

concepts.title: Adding integers — same and opposite signs

explanations.oneLine: Same-sign integers add and keep the sign; opposite-sign integers partly cancel (positive and negative tokens form zero pairs), and the larger-magnitude sign wins.
explanations.kidFriendly: Picture a carrom coin at 0, struck along a number line: rightward is positive, leftward negative. Strike +4 then +3 and it lands at +7 — same direction, distances add. Strike +5 then −3 and the leftward strike undoes part of the rightward: you land at +2. The token model makes it crisp: a positive token and a negative token form a 'zero pair' that cancels to nothing. So (+5) + (−3): pair three of the five positives with the three negatives — they vanish — leaving +2. Same signs: add and keep the sign. Opposite signs: cancel in pairs; whatever sign has more tokens left wins.
explanations.textbook: Integer addition: integers of the same sign add in magnitude, retaining the common sign: (+4)+(+3)=+7, (−4)+(−3)=−7. Integers of opposite sign partially cancel — a positive unit and a negative unit form a zero pair summing to 0 — and the result takes the sign of the larger-magnitude addend with magnitude equal to the difference: (+5)+(−3)=+2, (−5)+(+3)=−2. The number line (or token) model realises this.
explanations.expert: Integer addition is the group operation of (ℤ,+). The zero-pair cancellation embodies the additive inverse axiom a+(−a)=0; same-sign addition is magnitude addition under a common sign, opposite-sign is the signed difference. On the number line, adding b translates by b (rightward if b>0). This structure makes (ℤ,+) an abelian group, the foundation for all later signed arithmetic.

concepts.reasoning: Going the same way twice covers more ground in that direction — distances add, sign stays. Going opposite ways means the second move undoes part of the first; the cancellation is a positive and negative pairing off to zero, and whichever direction had 'more' determines where you end up.

useCases.description: Up 4 floors then down 3: net +1 floor.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The 'zero pair' idea — a positive and a negative annihilating to nothing — is exactly how physicists describe matter meeting antimatter, and how accountants net credits against debits. This simple cancellation is one of the most reused ideas across science and finance.
concepts.mnemonic: Same sign: add, keep sign. Opposite signs: cancel in pairs; bigger side's sign wins.
concepts.predictQuestion: A carrom coin at 0 is struck +5 (right) then −3 (left). Where does it end up, and how do 'zero pairs' explain it?
whyChain: Model rightward strikes as positive, leftward as negative. The first strike sends the coin to +5. The second, −3, pushes it 3 units back left, partly undoing the first move — landing at +2.

The token model makes the cancellation precise. Represent +5 as five positive tokens and −3 as three negative tokens. Each positive paired with a negative is a 'zero pair' that cancels to nothing. Three such pairs vanish, leaving 5 − 3 = 2 positive tokens: the result is +2.

This gives the general rule. Same-sign integers just stack — distances add, sign unchanged (+4 then +3 → +7). Opposite signs cancel in zero pairs, and whichever sign has tokens left over determines the result's sign and size. The zero-pair idea — a positive and negative annihilating — is the additive-inverse axiom a + (−a) = 0, and it reappears everywhere from accounting (credits vs debits) to physics (matter vs antimatter).

concepts.title: Properties of integer addition

explanations.oneLine: Integer addition is commutative and associative, has identity 0, and every integer has an opposite (additive inverse) that sums with it to 0.
explanations.kidFriendly: Integer addition behaves beautifully. You can add in any ORDER (commutative): (−3) + 5 = 5 + (−3) = 2. You can GROUP however you like (associative). Adding 0 changes nothing: 7 + 0 = 7 (0 is the identity). And every integer has an OPPOSITE that cancels it: 6 + (−6) = 0, (−6) + 6 = 0. These four properties — order-free, group-free, a do-nothing 0, and a canceling opposite for everyone — make integers a complete, reliable number system for adding. They're the same properties whole numbers had, plus the new power that EVERY integer (not just some) can be 'undone' by adding its opposite.
explanations.textbook: Integer addition satisfies: commutativity (a+b=b+a), associativity ((a+b)+c=a+(b+c)), additive identity (a+0=a), and additive inverse (a+(−a)=0 for every a). The existence of an inverse for every integer is the key advance over whole numbers, where only 0 had an inverse. These properties let any integer sum be rearranged and regrouped freely.
explanations.expert: (ℤ,+,0) is an abelian group: closure, associativity, identity 0, inverses (−a), and commutativity. The inverse axiom is precisely what whole numbers (ℕ,+) lack, making ℤ the 'completion' of ℕ under subtraction. This group structure underlies modular arithmetic, vector spaces, and essentially all of algebra.

concepts.reasoning: Adding combines amounts, and combining doesn't care about order or grouping — same as for whole numbers. What's new with integers is that every number now has a mirror-image opposite, so any addition can be exactly undone by adding that opposite.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The leap from whole numbers to integers is exactly the leap to a system where subtraction always works — because subtracting is just adding the opposite, and now every number HAS an opposite. This 'closure under subtraction' is why integers were invented and why they make algebra possible.
concepts.mnemonic: Add in any order/grouping; 0 does nothing; every integer has an opposite summing to 0.
concepts.predictQuestion: What makes integers better than whole numbers for addition — what new property does every integer have?
whyChain: Integer addition keeps all the friendly properties whole numbers had: you can add in any order (commutative), group terms any way (associative), and adding 0 changes nothing (identity). Those make sums easy to rearrange.

The genuinely NEW power is the additive inverse: every integer has an opposite that cancels it to zero — 6 + (−6) = 0, (−40) + 40 = 0. Whole numbers didn't have this; only 0 could cancel itself. Now EVERY number has a partner that undoes it.

This single new property is why integers were invented. Subtraction becomes 'adding the opposite', and since every integer now has an opposite, subtraction ALWAYS works — you can compute 3 − 7 and get −4 instead of being stuck. This 'closure under subtraction' is what makes integers a complete system for adding and subtracting, and it's the foundation that makes algebra possible.

concepts.title: Subtracting integers — adding the opposite

explanations.oneLine: To subtract an integer, add its opposite: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8, and 5 − 3 = 5 + (−3) = 2.
explanations.kidFriendly: Subtraction of integers has one golden rule: subtracting a number is the same as ADDING its opposite. So 5 − 3 becomes 5 + (−3) = 2. And the tricky one, 5 − (−3), becomes 5 + (+3) = 8 — subtracting a negative actually ADDS! Think of it on the carrom number line: subtracting means facing the opposite way. Or think of debt: taking away a ₹3 debt (−3) leaves you ₹3 better off. Once every subtraction is rewritten as 'add the opposite', you never need a separate set of subtraction rules — the addition rules you already know handle everything.
explanations.textbook: Subtraction of integers is defined as addition of the additive inverse: a − b = a + (−b). Thus 5 − 3 = 5 + (−3) = 2 and 5 − (−3) = 5 + (+3) = 8. Rewriting every subtraction as 'add the opposite' reduces all subtraction to the already-established rules of integer addition, and explains why subtracting a negative increases the value.
explanations.expert: In the additive group (ℤ,+), subtraction is not a primitive operation but the composition a − b := a + (−b), where −b is the unique additive inverse of b. This is why ℤ is closed under subtraction while ℕ is not: every element has an inverse. The identity a − (−b) = a + b is double-negation (−(−b) = b), and it underlies sign-handling throughout algebra.

concepts.reasoning: Subtraction asks 'what's left after removing b'. Removing b has the same effect as adding the opposite of b: removing a gain is a loss, and removing a loss (a negative) is a gain. So a − b and a + (−b) always land on the same place.

useCases.title: Temperature drop
useCases.description: From 5°C the temperature falls to −3°C: change = (−3) − 5 = −8°.

useCases.title: Cancelling a debt
useCases.description: Removing a ₹3 debt: balance − (−3) = balance + 3, you're ₹3 better off.

useCases.title: Lift movement
useCases.description: Going from floor 2 to floor −1 (basement) is a change of (−1) − 2 = −3 floors.

concepts.beyondTheBook: This 'subtract = add the opposite' rule is why calculators and computers don't need separate subtraction circuitry — they negate the second number and add. In binary, negation uses 'two's complement', and subtraction is literally implemented as addition of the complement. One unifying idea removes a whole operation.
concepts.mnemonic: Subtracting = adding the opposite. Keep-Change-Change: keep the first, change − to +, change the sign of the second.
concepts.predictQuestion: What is 5 − (−3), and why does subtracting a negative make the answer bigger?
whyChain: Subtraction undoes addition: a − b is the number you add to b to get a. The cleanest way to compute it is to notice that removing b has exactly the same effect as adding b's opposite. Take away a gain and you're worse off; take away a loss and you're better off.

So we DEFINE a − b = a + (−b). This turns every subtraction into an addition, meaning the integer-addition rules you already learned (same signs add, opposite signs cancel) handle subtraction too — no new rules needed. 5 − 3 = 5 + (−3) = 2; 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8.

The surprising case, subtracting a negative, now makes sense: −(−3) is +3 (double negation), so 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8, bigger than 5. Removing a debt is a gain. This single identity is why integers are closed under subtraction (every number has an opposite to add) and why computers implement subtraction as addition of a complement.

questions.prompt: A carrom coin at 0 is struck +5 then −3. Find its final position. Then find (−5) + (+3).
solutionSteps: +5 then −3: opposite signs cancel in pairs. 5 − 3 = 2, and the larger side is positive → +2.
(−5)+(+3): cancel 3 pairs, 5−3 = 2 left, larger side negative → −2.
commonMistakes: Adding magnitudes (5+3=8) for opposite signs.
Getting the resulting sign backwards.

questions.prompt: Compute (−8) + (+5) using the zero-pair idea.
solutionSteps: Pair 5 positives with 5 negatives → 5 zero pairs vanish.
commonMistakes: Answering +3 (wrong sign — more negatives remain).
Adding to get −13 (that's same-sign behaviour).

solutionSteps: All tokens pair off — a zero pair total.

questions.prompt: What is the additive inverse (opposite) of −12, and what do you get when you add an integer to its opposite?
questions.answer: The opposite of −12 is +12. Adding any integer to its opposite gives 0.
solutionSteps: The opposite of a number has the same size but the other sign: opposite of −12 is +12.
An integer plus its opposite cancels completely: −12 + 12 = 0.
This works for every integer (additive inverse property).
commonMistakes: Saying the opposite of −12 is −12.
Thinking only some integers have opposites.

solutionSteps: A number plus its opposite is 0.

questions.prompt: Compute 5 − (−3) by rewriting subtraction as adding the opposite.
solutionSteps: Subtracting a number = adding its opposite: 5 − (−3) = 5 + (+3).
commonMistakes: Writing 5 − 3 = 2 (forgetting the inner number is negative).
Thinking subtracting always makes the answer smaller — subtracting a negative makes it bigger.

questions.prompt: The temperature falls from 5 °C to −3 °C. What is the change in temperature?
solutionSteps: Same signs add, keep the sign: −8. So the change is −8 °C (a drop of 8 degrees).
commonMistakes: Computing 5 − 3 = 2 and ignoring the signs.
Getting +8 instead of −8 (the temperature dropped, so the change is negative).

variations.prompt: A lift goes from floor 2 to basement floor −1. Change in floors?

topics.title: Multiplying Integers & Sign Rules
topics.summary: Using the token-bag model — a positive multiplier puts tokens in, a negative multiplier takes them out — the sign rules emerge: positive × positive = positive, positive × negative = negative, and negative × negative = positive. Multiplication stays commutative whatever the signs.

concepts.title: The sign rules for multiplication

explanations.oneLine: Positive × positive = positive; positive × negative (or negative × positive) = negative; negative × negative = positive. The size is always the product of the magnitudes.
explanations.kidFriendly: Use a token bag. 4 × 2 means 'put 2 positives in, 4 times' → 8 positives = +8. 4 × (−2) means 'put 2 NEGATIVES in, 4 times' → 8 negatives = −8 (positive × negative = negative). What about (−4) × 2? A negative multiplier means REMOVE tokens: 'remove 2 positives, 4 times'. From an empty bag you first add zero pairs, then remove the positives, leaving 8 negatives = −8. And (−4) × (−2)? Remove 2 NEGATIVES four times — removing negatives leaves positives behind: +8! That's why negative × negative = positive. The magnitudes always just multiply (4 × 2 = 8); only the sign follows the rules.
explanations.textbook: Integer multiplication sign rules: (+)(+)=+, (+)(−)=−, (−)(+)=−, (−)(−)=+; the magnitude of the product is the product of the magnitudes. In the token model, a positive multiplier adds groups of tokens and a negative multiplier removes them (via zero pairs); removing negative tokens leaves positives, which is why (−)(−)=+. Multiplication remains commutative: a×b=b×a regardless of signs.
explanations.expert: The sign rules follow from requiring multiplication to distribute over addition consistently with a·0=0: from a·(b+(−b))=0 one derives a·(−b)=−(a·b), and (−a)·(−b)=a·b. This makes (ℤ,+,·) a commutative ring. The token 'removal' model is a concrete realisation of the additive-inverse interaction; the rules are forced, not arbitrary, by the ring axioms.

concepts.reasoning: A positive multiplier means 'add this group, this many times'; a negative multiplier means 'remove this group, that many times'. Removing positives leaves a deficit (negative); removing negatives takes away debt, leaving a surplus (positive). So two negatives multiplied give a positive.

useCases.title: Debt cancelled repeatedly
useCases.description: Removing a ₹2 debt 4 times improves your balance by +8: (−4)×(−2)=+8.

useCases.title: Reversing a downward trend
useCases.description: A −2°/hour cooling, considered 4 hours in the PAST (−4), means it was +8° warmer.

useCases.title: Direction × time
useCases.description: Moving −2 m/s for −4 s (time before now) = +8 m position earlier.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Why 'two negatives make a positive' confuses everyone at first — but the token-removal model makes it inevitable: taking away negatives is a positive change. This rule isn't a convention chosen for convenience; it's forced by requiring multiplication to play nicely with addition (the distributive law), which is one of the deepest demands in all of algebra.
concepts.mnemonic: Magnitudes multiply; signs follow: same signs → +, different signs → −.
concepts.predictQuestion: Using the token-bag model, why does (−4) × (−2) come out positive?
whyChain: In the token-bag model, a positive multiplier means 'put this group of tokens IN, that many times', while a negative multiplier means 'REMOVE this group, that many times'. So 4 × (−2) puts in 2 negatives four times → −8.

Now (−4) × (−2): the −4 says remove the group four times, and the group is 2 NEGATIVE tokens. To remove negatives from an empty bag, first add zero pairs (a positive and negative together, summing to 0), then take the negatives away. Removing the negatives leaves their positive partners behind. Doing this four times leaves 8 positive tokens — so (−4) × (−2) = +8.

That's why two negatives multiply to a positive: removing negatives is a positive change. The magnitudes simply multiply (4 × 2 = 8); only the sign follows the rules (same signs → +, different → −). And this isn't an arbitrary convention — it's forced by requiring multiplication to distribute over addition, one of the deepest consistency demands in algebra.

solutionSteps: Magnitudes multiply; signs follow the rules.
commonMistakes: Getting (−4)×(−2) = −8 (two negatives give a POSITIVE).
Mismatching magnitudes (e.g. 4×6 = 10).

questions.prompt: State the four sign rules for multiplying integers.
questions.answer: (+)(+)=+, (+)(−)=−, (−)(+)=−, (−)(−)=+. The magnitude is always the product of the magnitudes.
solutionSteps: Same signs give a positive product: (+)(+)=+ and (−)(−)=+.
Different signs give a negative product: (+)(−)=− and (−)(+)=−.
In every case, multiply the magnitudes for the size.
commonMistakes: Thinking (−)(−)=− .
Forgetting that the size is just the product of magnitudes.

questions.prompt: Is (−6) × 3 equal to 3 × (−6)? What property does this show?
questions.answer: Yes — both equal −18. This shows integer multiplication is commutative (swapping the order doesn't change the product or its sign).
solutionSteps: Equal — multiplication is commutative for integers, signs included.
commonMistakes: Thinking the order changes the sign.
Computing different magnitudes for the two orders.

variations.prompt: Sign of the product when multiplier and multiplicand swap?

glossary.definition: A whole number that may be positive, negative, or zero.
A line with 0 in the middle, positives to the right and negatives to the left.
A positive and a negative token together, summing to 0.
The number with the same size but opposite sign; it sums with the original to 0.
Order doesn't change the result: a+b=b+a and a×b=b×a.
Grouping doesn't change the result of addition (or multiplication).
The size of a number ignoring its sign.
Same signs give a positive product; different signs give a negative product.
Using green (positive) and red (negative) tokens to model integer operations.
A number that leaves others unchanged: 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication.

mnemonics.unpacking: Adding same-sign integers: add and keep the sign. Opposite signs: cancel in zero pairs; the bigger side's sign wins.
mnemonics.context: Use for adding integers.

mnemonics.unpacking: Multiplying: same signs give a positive product, different signs give a negative product. Magnitudes always multiply.
mnemonics.context: Use for the multiplication sign rules.

mnemonics.unpacking: In the token model, removing negative tokens leaves positives — which is why (−)×(−) = +.
mnemonics.context: Use to remember why two negatives make a positive.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Adding two integers always makes a bigger number.
misconceptions.actually: Adding a negative makes it smaller: (+5)+(−3)=+2, less than 5. Opposite signs partly cancel.

misconceptions.kidsThink: (−)×(−) = − (two negatives make a negative).
misconceptions.actually: (−)×(−) = + . Removing negative tokens leaves positives; two negatives multiplied give a POSITIVE.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Subtraction is different from addition for integers.
misconceptions.actually: Subtracting is adding the opposite: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8. Every subtraction is an addition in disguise.

misconceptions.kidsThink: The sign of a product depends on which number is bigger.
misconceptions.actually: It depends only on the SIGNS: same signs → +, different → −. Magnitude just sets the size.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Only zero has an opposite.
misconceptions.actually: EVERY integer has an opposite (additive inverse): the opposite of −12 is 12, of 7 is −7. This is what makes subtraction always possible.

realWorldExamples.title: Bank balances go both ways
realWorldExamples.body: A deposit is a positive integer, a withdrawal a negative one. Deposit ₹500 then withdraw ₹300: (+500)+(−300) = +200 change. Withdraw more than you have and the balance goes negative — integers are exactly the maths of money that can go below zero.

realWorldExamples.title: Why removing debt is a gain
realWorldExamples.body: If a ₹2 debt is cancelled (removed) 4 times, your balance rises by ₹8: (−4)×(−2) = +8. The puzzling 'negative times negative is positive' is just 'taking away something bad makes things better', four times over.

realWorldExamples.title: Temperatures above and below zero
realWorldExamples.body: In Shimla in January the temperature might be +3° at noon and fall to −4° at night — a change of −7°. Integer addition and subtraction describe every rise and fall across the zero of the freezing point.

ncertQA.question: A carrom coin at 0 is struck 4 units right, then 3 units right. Where does it end up, and what is the general formula for two same-direction strikes a and b?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: It ends at 4 + 3 = 7 units from 0. In general the final position is P = a + b.

ncertQA.question: Compute (+5) + (−3) and (−5) + (+3) using zero pairs.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: (+5)+(−3): three zero pairs cancel, leaving +2. (−5)+(+3): three zero pairs cancel, leaving −2. Opposite signs partly cancel; the larger-magnitude sign remains.

ncertQA.question: What is the additive inverse of an integer, and give the inverse of −12.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: The additive inverse of a number is the number with the same magnitude but opposite sign; it sums with the original to 0. The inverse of −12 is +12, since −12 + 12 = 0.

ncertQA.question: Using the token model, what is 4 × (−2)?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: 4 × (−2) means placing 2 negative tokens into an empty bag 4 times, giving 8 negatives, i.e. −8.

ncertQA.question: Why is (−4) × (−2) equal to +8?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: A negative multiplier means removing tokens. (−4) × (−2) removes 2 negative tokens four times; removing negatives (after laying down zero pairs) leaves their positive partners, giving 8 positives, i.e. +8.

ncertQA.question: State the sign rules for multiplying two integers.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: (+)(+)=+, (+)(−)=−, (−)(+)=−, (−)(−)=+. Same signs give a positive product, different signs a negative product; the magnitude is the product of the magnitudes.

ncertQA.question: Does swapping the multiplier and multiplicand change the product's sign?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: No. Multiplication is commutative: a × b = b × a for all integers, and the sign is the same before and after swapping (same-sign stays +, different-sign stays −).

ncertQA.question: Compute (−9) × 7 and 8 × (−3).

miniProjects.title: Token-Bag Integer Machine
needs: Two colours of small counters (or paper circles) — say green for +1 and red for −1
steps: Model addition: to compute (+5)+(−3), put 5 green and 3 red into the bag; remove every green-red 'zero pair'; count what's left.
Record the result and its sign. Repeat for (−6)+(+2), (+4)+(+3), (−5)+(−1).
Model multiplication: for 4×(−2), put 2 reds in, four times; count the result.
For (−4)×(−2): lay down zero pairs, then REMOVE 2 reds four times; count the greens left over.
Write the sign rule you discover for each kind of product.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: Zero pairs cancel cleanly in addition; in multiplication, removing red (negative) tokens leaves green (positive) ones — so (−)×(−) comes out positive, just as the sign rule says.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: The tokens make additive inverses physical: a green and a red sum to zero. A negative multiplier means 'remove', and removing negatives leaves positives behind — a hands-on demonstration that two negatives multiply to a positive, forced by how addition and removal interact.

chapters.title: Finding Common Ground
chapters.summary: Sameeksha wants the largest square tile that fits a 12 ft by 16 ft room exactly — that's the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of 12 and 16. When two bells ring at different intervals, when do they ring together? That's the Least Common Multiple (LCM). This chapter finds HCF and LCM, the prime-factorisation method, and the elegant fact that HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers.

topics.title: Highest Common Factor (HCF)
topics.summary: The HCF (or GCD) of two numbers is the largest number that divides both. The biggest square tile fitting a 12×16 room has side = HCF(12,16) = 4 ft, because the tile side must be a common factor of both dimensions, and we want the largest.

concepts.title: HCF — the greatest common factor

explanations.oneLine: The Highest Common Factor (HCF, also GCD) of two numbers is the largest number that divides both exactly.
explanations.kidFriendly: Sameeksha tiles a 12 ft × 16 ft room with the largest possible equal square tiles, whole-foot sides, fewest tiles. The tile side must divide 12 exactly (to fit the breadth) AND divide 16 exactly (to fit the length) — so it must be a COMMON factor of 12 and 16. Factors of 12: 1,2,3,4,6,12. Factors of 16: 1,2,4,8,16. Common ones: 1, 2, 4. The LARGEST is 4 — so 4 ft tiles, the fewest. This largest common factor is the Highest Common Factor (HCF), also called the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD). HCF(12,16) = 4.
explanations.textbook: The Highest Common Factor (HCF) — equivalently the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) — of two or more numbers is the greatest number that divides each of them exactly. It is found by listing common factors and taking the largest, or via prime factorisation (product of common prime factors to the lowest power). For 12 and 16: common factors 1, 2, 4; HCF = 4.
explanations.expert: The GCD of a, b generates the ideal (a,b) in ℤ; gcd(a,b) is the smallest positive integer expressible as ax+by (Bézout). It equals the product of shared primes to minimum exponents. The Euclidean algorithm computes it in O(log) steps via gcd(a,b)=gcd(b, a mod b). The GCD is foundational to number theory, fraction reduction, and modular inverses.

concepts.reasoning: A tile must fit both room dimensions with no gaps, so its side has to divide both — a common factor. To use the fewest tiles, you want each tile as big as possible, so you take the GREATEST common factor.

useCases.title: Largest square tile
useCases.description: Biggest tile for a 12×16 room is 4 ft (= HCF) — fewest tiles, exact fit.

useCases.title: Equal-size packing
useCases.description: 84 kg and 108 kg of rice in equal bags (one farm each): bag size = HCF(84,108).

useCases.title: Reducing fractions
useCases.description: To simplify 12/16, divide both by HCF 4 → 3/4.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The HCF is what you divide by to reduce a fraction to lowest terms — 12/16 ÷ 4/4 = 3/4. The Euclidean algorithm for computing GCD is over 2,000 years old (in Euclid's Elements) and is still used inside modern cryptography (RSA) every time you make a secure connection online.
concepts.mnemonic: HCF = the BIGGEST number dividing both. Common factor, greatest of them.
concepts.predictQuestion: Sameeksha tiles a 12 ft by 16 ft room with the largest equal square tiles (whole-foot sides). What size should the tiles be, and why?
whyChain: For square tiles to fit a 12 ft by 16 ft room exactly with no gaps, each tile's side must divide BOTH dimensions evenly — it has to be a common factor of 12 and 16. The factors of 12 are 1,2,3,4,6,12; of 16 are 1,2,4,8,16; the common ones are 1, 2 and 4.
Sameeksha wants the FEWEST tiles, which means the biggest tiles — so she takes the LARGEST common factor, 4. Tiles of side 4 ft fit exactly (12 = 3×4, 16 = 4×4) and use the fewest pieces.

That largest common factor is the Highest Common Factor (HCF), also called the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD): HCF(12,16) = 4. The same idea reduces fractions (12/16 ÷ 4 = 3/4) and, via the 2,000-year-old Euclidean algorithm, even powers the cryptography behind every secure website.

questions.prompt: Find the HCF of 12 and 16.
commonMistakes: Picking a common factor that isn't the largest (e.g. 2).
Listing a multiple instead of a factor.

questions.prompt: Lekhana has 84 kg of rice from one farm and 108 kg from another. She packs equal bags, each with rice from only one farm, using the largest possible bag size. What bag size, and how many bags?
solutionSteps: Bag size must divide both 84 and 108 → a common factor; largest gives fewest bags → HCF.
commonMistakes: Using a smaller common factor (more bags than needed).
Adding 84+108 first instead of treating farms separately.

How many 12 kg bags from 108 kg?

topics.title: Least Common Multiple (LCM)
topics.summary: The LCM of two numbers is the smallest number that both divide into — the smallest common multiple. If one bell rings every 6 minutes and another every 8, they ring together every LCM(6,8) = 24 minutes. It's found from the multiples, or faster from prime factorisation.

concepts.title: LCM — the least common multiple

explanations.oneLine: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two numbers is the smallest number that is a multiple of both.
explanations.kidFriendly: Two bells: one rings every 6 minutes, the other every 8. They just rang together — when do they next ring together? You need a time that is a multiple of BOTH 6 and 8. Multiples of 6: 6,12,18,24,30… Multiples of 8: 8,16,24,32… The smallest shared one is 24. So they ring together every 24 minutes. This smallest common multiple is the Least Common Multiple (LCM). LCM(6,8) = 24. Unlike HCF (which is about dividing INTO numbers), LCM is about the smallest number these go into — useful for 'when do repeating events line up?' and for adding fractions with different denominators.
explanations.textbook: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers is the smallest positive number that is a multiple of each. It is found by listing multiples and taking the smallest common one, or via prime factorisation (product of all primes present to the highest power). For 6 and 8: 6 = 2·3, 8 = 2³, so LCM = 2³·3 = 24.
explanations.expert: The LCM is the join in the divisibility lattice; lcm(a,b) = product of primes to maximum exponents. It is the generator of the intersection ideal (a)∩(b). The identity gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = a·b links the two. LCM underlies the common denominator in ℚ and the period of combined cyclic events (Chinese Remainder contexts).

concepts.reasoning: Events that repeat at different intervals line up again only at a time both intervals divide into evenly — a common multiple. The FIRST time they coincide is the smallest such number, the least common multiple.

useCases.title: Bells ringing together
useCases.description: Bells every 6 and 8 min coincide every LCM = 24 min.

useCases.title: Adding fractions
useCases.description: To add 1/6 + 1/8, use the common denominator LCM(6,8) = 24.

useCases.title: Traffic-light cycles
useCases.description: Two lights with 6 s and 8 s cycles sync every 24 s.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The LCM is exactly the common denominator you need when adding fractions like 1/6 + 1/8 — rewrite both over 24. It also governs real cyclic phenomena: when planets align, when shift rosters repeat, when gears return to their start. 'When do repeating cycles coincide?' is always an LCM question.
concepts.mnemonic: LCM = the SMALLEST number both go into. Useful for lining up repeating cycles.
concepts.predictQuestion: One bell rings every 6 minutes, another every 8. If they ring together now, after how many minutes do they next ring together?
whyChain: For both bells to ring at the same moment, the elapsed time must be a multiple of 6 (for the first bell) AND a multiple of 8 (for the second) — a COMMON multiple of 6 and 8.

List them: multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, …; multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, …. The smallest shared value is 24. So the bells next coincide after 24 minutes — that's the Least Common Multiple, LCM(6,8) = 24.

Notice how LCM differs from HCF: HCF is the biggest number that divides INTO both (for splitting into equal parts), while LCM is the smallest number both divide into (for when repeating things line up). LCM is exactly the common denominator for adding 1/6 + 1/8, and it governs every 'when do cycles coincide?' question — synced traffic lights, repeating rosters, aligning gears.

questions.prompt: Find the LCM of 6 and 8.
commonMistakes: Picking 48 (a common multiple, but not the LEAST).
Confusing with HCF (which would be 2).

questions.prompt: Two traffic lights have cycles of 6 seconds and 8 seconds. They turn green together now. After how long do they next turn green together?
questions.answer: 24 seconds (LCM of 6 and 8).
solutionSteps: They sync at a common multiple of 6 and 8.
So they next turn green together after 24 seconds.
commonMistakes: Adding 6 + 8 = 14 instead of finding the LCM.
Using HCF (2) instead of LCM.

variations.prompt: Bells every 9 and 12 min — when do they coincide?

topics.title: HCF, LCM and Prime Factorisation
topics.summary: Break each number into its prime building blocks. The HCF takes the common primes to the LOWEST power; the LCM takes all primes to the HIGHEST power. And there's a pretty shortcut: HCF × LCM always equals the product of the two numbers.

concepts.title: Prime factorisation and the HCF×LCM relationship

explanations.oneLine: Using prime factorisation, HCF takes common primes to the lowest power and LCM takes all primes to the highest power; always, HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.
explanations.kidFriendly: Break numbers into prime building blocks. 12 = 2² × 3, 18 = 2 × 3². For the HCF, take each shared prime to its LOWEST power: 2¹ × 3¹ = 6. For the LCM, take every prime to its HIGHEST power: 2² × 3² = 36. Now the pretty fact: HCF × LCM = 6 × 36 = 216, and 12 × 18 = 216 too! For ANY two numbers, HCF × LCM = their product. This means once you know one, you can find the other: if you have the HCF, then LCM = (product) ÷ HCF. Prime factorisation makes both HCF and LCM fast, and the relationship ties them together beautifully.
explanations.textbook: Via prime factorisation, the HCF is the product of common prime factors raised to the minimum exponent, and the LCM is the product of all prime factors raised to the maximum exponent. For any two positive integers a, b: HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b. Hence LCM = (a×b)/HCF, allowing one to be computed from the other.
explanations.expert: By unique factorisation, writing a = ∏ p^{e_i}, b = ∏ p^{f_i}, gcd = ∏ p^{min(e_i,f_i)} and lcm = ∏ p^{max(e_i,f_i)}. Since min+max = e+f for each prime, gcd·lcm = ∏ p^{e_i+f_i} = a·b. This identity, plus the Euclidean algorithm for gcd, gives an efficient lcm computation without full factorisation.

concepts.reasoning: Each number is a product of prime powers. A factor common to both can only use primes both have, and only as many copies as the SMALLER has — that's the HCF. A multiple of both must include enough copies for the LARGER — that's the LCM. Because min + max of each prime's powers equals the total, the product HCF × LCM rebuilds a × b exactly.

useCases.title: Quick LCM from HCF
useCases.description: HCF(12,18)=6, so LCM = 12×18/6 = 36 — no listing needed.

useCases.title: Reducing and combining fractions
useCases.description: Prime factors give both the HCF (to reduce) and LCM (to add) of denominators.

useCases.title: Gear teeth alignment
useCases.description: Prime factors of two gears' tooth counts give when they realign (LCM).

concepts.beyondTheBook: The HCF × LCM = product identity is a gift: it turns a hard LCM into an easy division once you have the (easier) HCF. Prime factorisation itself — the fact that every number breaks into primes in exactly one way (the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) — is one of the cornerstones of all mathematics.
concepts.mnemonic: HCF: common primes, lowest power. LCM: all primes, highest power. HCF × LCM = a × b.
concepts.predictQuestion: Using 12 = 2²×3 and 18 = 2×3², what are the HCF and LCM, and does HCF × LCM equal 12 × 18?
whyChain: Write each number in primes: 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3². The HCF keeps only the primes BOTH share, each to the LOWEST power present: 2¹ × 3¹ = 6. The LCM keeps EVERY prime that appears, each to the HIGHEST power: 2² × 3² = 36.

Now check the relationship: HCF × LCM = 6 × 36 = 216, and 12 × 18 = 216 — they match. This is no coincidence: for every prime, min(power) + max(power) equals the sum of the two powers, so multiplying HCF and LCM rebuilds exactly a × b.

This identity is a practical gift. The HCF is usually easy (small common factors); once you have it, LCM = (a × b) ÷ HCF — no listing of multiples needed. And it all rests on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every number factors into primes in exactly one way, a cornerstone of mathematics.

questions.prompt: Find the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18 using prime factorisation.
questions.answer: 12 = 2²×3, 18 = 2×3². HCF = 2×3 = 6 (common primes, lowest power); LCM = 2²×3² = 36 (all primes, highest power).
solutionSteps: HCF: common primes to lowest power → 2¹·3¹ = 6.
LCM: all primes to highest power → 2²·3² = 36.
commonMistakes: Taking highest powers for HCF or lowest for LCM (swapped).
Missing a prime that appears in only one number when finding LCM.

questions.prompt: The HCF of two numbers is 6 and their product is 216. What is their LCM?
solutionSteps: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.
commonMistakes: Multiplying HCF by the product instead of dividing.
Forgetting the HCF×LCM = product relationship.

variations.prompt: LCM 60, HCF 5. Find the product of the numbers.

Writing a number as a product of prime numbers.
