concepts.beyondTheBook: This 'inverse operations, both sides' method is the heart of all equation-solving you'll do for years — through linear equations, simultaneous equations, and beyond. The same logic (undo operations in reverse, keep both sides equal) drives the algebra behind physics formulas, computer algorithms, and engineering. Master it here and it pays off everywhere.
concepts.mnemonic: Undo each operation with its inverse, on BOTH sides, until the unknown is alone.
concepts.predictQuestion: Solve 2n + 1 = 99 systematically. Which operations do you undo, and in what order?
whyChain: The unknown n has two operations wrapped around it: it's multiplied by 2, then 1 is added. To free n, undo these with INVERSE operations, peeling from the outside in — and to keep the equation true, do each step to BOTH sides (the balance rule).
The outermost operation is '+1', so undo it first: subtract 1 from both sides, giving 2n = 98. Now only the '×2' remains; undo it with its inverse, division: divide both sides by 2, giving n = 49.

Subtraction undid the addition, and division undid the multiplication — each inverse applied to both sides so the scale never tipped. This 'inverse operations on both sides, outermost first' method replaces slow trial-and-error and is the backbone of all equation-solving to come, from physics formulas to computer algorithms. A quick check (2×49+1 = 99 ✓) confirms it.

questions.prompt: Solve 2n + 1 = 99 systematically.
commonMistakes: Dividing by 2 before subtracting 1 (wrong order — peel the outermost first).
Doing the operation to only one side.

questions.prompt: Solve 5x − 4 = 7 (compare with how slow trial and error would be).
solutionSteps: Check: 5 × 2.2 − 4 = 11 − 4 = 7. ✓ Trial and error with whole numbers would have missed this non-whole answer.
commonMistakes: Subtracting 4 instead of adding (the inverse of −4 is +4).
Stopping at 5x = 11 without dividing.

questions.prompt: Why is doing the same operation to both sides allowed when solving an equation?
questions.answer: Because the two sides are equal (a balanced scale). Performing the same operation on equal quantities keeps them equal, just as removing equal weights from both pans keeps the scale balanced.
solutionSteps: An equation means LHS = RHS — the two sides have the same value.
If two quantities are equal and you do the same thing to both, they stay equal.
This mirrors a balanced scale staying balanced when equal weights are removed from both pans.
commonMistakes: Thinking you can operate on just one side.
Forgetting that the sides start out equal.

variations.prompt: Can you add 10 to only the left side?
variations.answer: No — that breaks the balance; add to both.

variations.prompt: Does dividing both sides by 2 keep 8 = 8 true?

topics.title: Checking Solutions & Common Mistakes
topics.summary: Always substitute your answer back to confirm the sides balance — it catches almost every slip. The usual mistakes: doing an operation to only one side, undoing operations in the wrong order, or mishandling a sign. A quick check turns a guess into a certainty.

concepts.title: Verify by substitution; mend common mistakes

explanations.oneLine: Substituting the solution back confirms it; the common slips are operating on one side only, wrong order of inverses, and sign errors.
explanations.kidFriendly: Once you've solved an equation, CHECK it: put your answer back in and see if both sides match. Solve 3x − 5 = 16 → x = 7? Check: 3 × 7 − 5 = 21 − 5 = 16. ✓ It works. This catches almost every mistake. The usual slips: (1) doing an operation to only ONE side (breaks the balance) — always do it to BOTH; (2) undoing operations in the wrong ORDER — peel the outermost first (undo +/− before ×/÷ that wraps the variable); (3) SIGN errors — the inverse of −5 is +5, not −5. 'Mind the mistake, mend the mistake': a ten-second substitution check is the cheapest insurance in all of maths.
explanations.textbook: Every solution should be verified by substituting it into the original equation and confirming LHS = RHS. Common errors: (1) applying an operation to only one side, destroying the equality; (2) undoing operations in the wrong order (the inverse operations should reverse the order of application); (3) sign errors when moving terms. Substitution-checking detects all of these reliably.
explanations.expert: Verification evaluates the original predicate at the computed root, independent of the solution path — catching transcription, order, and sign errors. The common faults correspond to applying a non-equivalence transformation (one-sided op), composing inverses out of order, or sign mismanagement in additive inverses. Checking restores soundness against these procedural lapses.

concepts.reasoning: Because solving is a chain of steps, a slip anywhere gives a wrong answer — but the original equation is the ultimate judge. Putting your answer back in tests it against that judge directly, exposing any error regardless of where it crept in.

concepts.beyondTheBook: 'Mind the mistake, mend the mistake' is a recurring NEP theme precisely because LEARNING to spot and fix your own errors is more valuable than never making them. The substitution check makes equations self-correcting — a habit that, carried into all of algebra and science, prevents a lifetime of avoidable errors.
concepts.mnemonic: Always substitute back to check. Watch for: one-sided ops, wrong order, sign slips.
concepts.predictQuestion: You solve 3x − 5 = 16 and get x = 7. How do you confirm it, and what are the three most common mistakes to watch for?
whyChain: Confirm by substitution: put x = 7 back into the ORIGINAL equation. The left side becomes 3 × 7 − 5 = 21 − 5 = 16, which equals the right side. The scale balances, so x = 7 is correct — verified independently of how you solved it.

The three classic slips a check catches: (1) operating on only ONE side — every operation must hit both sides or the balance breaks; (2) undoing operations in the WRONG ORDER — peel the outermost first, undoing +/− before the ×/÷ that wraps the variable; (3) SIGN errors — the inverse of −5 is +5, and dropping that sign is a frequent trap.

Because solving is a chain of steps, an error anywhere produces a wrong answer — but the original equation is the final judge, and substitution puts your answer straight in front of it. This 'mind the mistake, mend the mistake' habit makes equations self-correcting and is the cheapest insurance in all of mathematics.

questions.prompt: Solve 3x − 5 = 16 and verify your answer by substitution.
commonMistakes: Subtracting 5 (the inverse of −5 is +5).
Forgetting to verify.

questions.prompt: A student solves x + 8 = 20 by writing 'x = 20 + 8 = 28'. Find and mend the mistake.
questions.answer: Mistake: they ADDED 8 instead of subtracting it. To undo '+8' you subtract 8 from both sides: x = 20 − 8 = 12. Check: 12 + 8 = 20. ✓
solutionSteps: The equation is x + 8 = 20. To isolate x, undo the +8 with its inverse: subtract 8.
The student added 8 (wrong inverse). Correct answer x = 12.
commonMistakes: Using the same operation instead of the inverse.
Skipping the check that would have caught it (28 + 8 = 36 ≠ 20).

misconceptions.kidsThink: You can change just one side of an equation.
misconceptions.actually: You must do the SAME operation to BOTH sides, or the balance (equality) breaks.

misconceptions.kidsThink: To undo '+8' you add 8.
misconceptions.actually: You SUBTRACT 8 — the inverse of addition is subtraction. To undo +8, subtract 8 from both sides.

misconceptions.actually: Peel the OUTERMOST operation first: undo the +/− around the variable before the ×/÷ that multiplies it.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Trial and error is the best way to solve equations.
misconceptions.actually: It works but is slow and can miss non-whole answers (like x = 2.2). The systematic inverse-operations method is reliable and fast.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Once you get an answer you're done.
misconceptions.actually: Always SUBSTITUTE it back to check both sides match — it catches almost every mistake.

realWorldExamples.title: Working back from a total
realWorldExamples.body: If 3 identical items plus ₹20 delivery cost ₹110, the equation 3x + 20 = 110 finds each item's price: subtract 20 (3x = 90), divide by 3 (x = ₹30). Every 'I know the total, what was each part?' question is an equation waiting to be solved.

realWorldExamples.title: The balance scale of algebra
realWorldExamples.body: The equals sign was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde, who chose two parallel lines 'because no two things can be more equal'. Seeing an equation as a balanced scale — keep both sides equal — is the mental shift that turns arithmetic into algebra.

realWorldExamples.title: Self-checking with substitution
realWorldExamples.body: Engineers and scientists rearrange formulas constantly, then plug in test values to confirm the rearrangement is correct. The same substitution check you use on 3x − 5 = 16 guards multi-step calculations in the real world against costly errors.

ncertQA.question: A balanced scale has a sack of weight w plus 5 kg on the left and 12 kg on the right. Write and solve the equation.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: w + 5 = 12. Remove 5 kg from both pans (subtract 5 from both sides): w = 7 kg.

ncertQA.question: Solve 2n + 1 = 99 by trial and error, then check.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Testing values: n=40 gives 81, n=50 gives 101, n=49 gives 99. So n = 49. Trial and error works but is slow.

ncertQA.question: If LHS = RHS, will the equation still hold after adding the same number to both sides?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Yes. Since both sides have the same value, performing the same operation (adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing by the same number) on both keeps them equal.

ncertQA.question: Solve 2n + 1 = 99 systematically.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Subtract 1 from both sides: 2n = 98. Divide both sides by 2: n = 49. Check: 2×49+1 = 99.

ncertQA.question: Solve 5x − 4 = 7.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Add 4 to both sides: 5x = 11. Divide by 5: x = 11/5 = 2.2. Check: 5×2.2 − 4 = 7.

ncertQA.question: Why is doing the same operation to both sides justified?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Because the two sides are equal (like a balanced scale). Doing the same thing to equal quantities keeps them equal — exactly like removing equal weights from both pans of a balanced scale.

ncertQA.question: A student writes 'x + 8 = 20, so x = 20 + 8 = 28.' Mend the mistake.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: To undo +8, you SUBTRACT 8, not add it: x = 20 − 8 = 12. Check: 12 + 8 = 20. The error was using the wrong inverse operation.

ncertQA.question: Solve 3x − 5 = 16 and verify your answer.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: Add 5: 3x = 21. Divide by 3: x = 7. Verify: 3×7 − 5 = 21 − 5 = 16 = RHS. ✓

miniProjects.title: Build a Balance, Solve an Equation
needs: A ruler balanced on a pencil (a simple see-saw), or a drawing of a balance scale
A mystery item (e.g. a sealed envelope with hidden coins)
steps: Set up the balance with a mystery item plus some known coins on one side, and known coins on the other, so it balances.
Write the equation: mystery + (known) = (known), e.g. m + 3 = 8.
Remove the SAME number of coins from both sides and watch it stay balanced — until the mystery item is alone.
Read off the mystery weight (the solution), e.g. m = 5.
Now write a 'two-step' equation like 2m + 1 = 11, and solve it systematically (subtract 1 from both sides, then divide by 2), checking by substitution.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: Removing equal amounts from both sides keeps the balance level, and peeling them away leaves the mystery weight alone — exactly mirroring how subtracting and dividing both sides of an equation isolates the unknown.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: An equation is a balanced scale: both sides are equal. Any operation done equally to both sides preserves that equality, so inverse operations (subtract to undo add, divide to undo multiply) strip away everything around the unknown without ever tipping the balance — leaving the solution.

scientists.name: Brahmagupta
scientists.oneLineLegacy: Gave the first general method for solving linear and quadratic equations, and rules for zero and negative numbers.
scientists.narrative: Brahmagupta, working in 7th-century Rajasthan, was among the first mathematicians anywhere to treat equations with general methods rather than case-by-case tricks. In his Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta he stated rules for solving linear equations, handled negative quantities (debts) and zero as numbers, and gave a general solution to quadratic equations centuries before such methods reached Europe. The very idea of an 'unknown' to be found by systematic operations — the heart of this chapter — owes much to the Indian algebraic tradition he helped found. The word 'algebra' itself comes later from the Arabic al-jabr, but its roots reach back to scholars like Brahmagupta and, later, Bhāskara.
